## OET Writing: Referral Letter Structure | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-writing-referral-letter-structure.html

How to structure an OET Writing referral letter and choose which case notes to keep or omit, with a worked practice case, paragraph plan and model sentences.

OET Writing
OET Writing: referral letter structure and note selection
A referral letter asks a colleague to take action. This guide shows you how to decide which case notes the reader needs, which to leave out, and how to order the paragraphs so the request is clear from the first line to the last.
See the practice example
Get a letter marked
By Dr Ahmed Hesham , medical doctor and founder of OET with Dr Hesham · Published 27 Oct 2026
The referral route
Reader first, notes second, paragraphs third.
Every decision in a referral letter comes back to one question: what does this reader need in order to do what I am asking?
01 Name the request Who is the reader and what should they do?
02 Sort the notes Keep, summarise or omit each note.
03 Plan the paragraphs Most important information first.
What a referral letter has to do
The question many candidates ask is not "how do I start?" but "how much of the case notes should go in?" The answer depends on the reader and the request, not on the notes.
What OET actually asks for OET describes the Writing sub-test as a profession-specific task, such as a document of referral, advice, or a letter of transfer or discharge, written from case notes. You get 5 minutes of reading time, during which you cannot write or mark anything, and then 40 minutes to write. You can look at the case notes at any point during the 40 minutes.
Length is a guide, not the goal OET gives a guide of 180–200 words for the body of the letter and says assessors do not count your words. They check whether you have included what the reader needs and left out what they do not. A long referral is almost always a selection problem.
The six criteria behind every decision Your letter is scored on Purpose, Content, Conciseness & Clarity, Genre & Style, Organisation & Layout, and Language. Note selection feeds Content and Conciseness & Clarity directly, and paragraph order is what Organisation & Layout rewards.
What makes a referral different In a discharge or transfer letter you hand over ongoing care. In a referral you ask someone, often a specialist, to assess or treat a problem you cannot resolve yourself. The reader must understand within the first paragraph why the patient is coming to them, and everything after that should justify the request.
A five-step method: from case notes to paragraph plan
Use the reading time for steps 1 to 3 in your head, then spend the first few minutes of writing time on steps 4 and 5. OET itself suggests using the first 2–3 minutes of writing time to plan.
1. Name the reader and the request
Read the task box before the notes. Write one sentence in your head: "I want this specialist to assess X because Y." That sentence becomes your opening paragraph and your filter for every note.
2. Sort every note into three groups
Essential: the reader cannot act without it. Supporting: it helps the reader understand the problem or plan safely. Omit: it is irrelevant to this request, already known to the reader, or resolved.
3. Merge what repeats
Case notes often record the same problem at several visits. The reader needs the trend, not each entry. Turn three peak-flow readings or three blood pressures into one sentence that shows the direction of change.
4. Choose chronological or thematic order
If the story is a routine timeline, dated paragraphs work well. If the current problem matters most, group by theme: the problem now, what has been tried, relevant background. OET notes there is no fixed number of paragraphs.
5. Put the key sentence first
Inside each paragraph, lead with the most important sentence. Then close the letter by repeating the request clearly, so the reader finishes knowing exactly what you want them to do.
Practice example: selecting notes for a respiratory referral
This is an invented practice case written by OET with Dr Hesham to demonstrate the method. It is not an official OET task and does not describe a real patient.
Practice example: the task You are a GP at Riverside Surgery. Write a letter of referral to Dr Helen Marsh, Consultant Respiratory Physician, City Hospital, requesting specialist assessment of Mr Brennan’s asthma.
Practice example: case notes (summary)
Mr Tom Brennan, 47, warehouse supervisor; lives with wife and two teenage children
Asthma since childhood; hay fever (cetirizine 10 mg PRN); appendicectomy 1998; NKDA
Ex-smoker: 10/day for 20 years, quit 2019; pet cat for 8 years
Meds: beclometasone/formoterol 100/6, 2 puffs BD; salbutamol 100 mcg PRN
12/08: night cough 3–4 nights/week, salbutamol daily; inhaler technique corrected; peak flow 380 L/min (predicted 560)
28/08: A&E attendance with exacerbation; prednisolone 40 mg for 5 days
09/09: symptoms unchanged; repeat prescriptions confirm good adherence; peak flow 360 L/min
14/10: still waking at night; 4 days off work in September; stopped five-a-side football; BP 128/82; flu vaccine given
Keep, because the specialist needs it
Night symptoms and daily reliever use: the evidence of poor control
Peak flow falling from 380 to 360 L/min against a predicted 560: one sentence, not two
The A&E exacerbation and oral steroid course
Current inhalers, corrected technique and confirmed adherence: shows the problem is not simply technique or compliance
Ex-smoker, pet cat and hay fever: possible contributing factors the specialist will consider
Time off work and stopping football: the impact on daily life
Omit, because it does not change the request
Appendicectomy in 1998: unrelated and resolved
Normal blood pressure and the flu vaccine: routine, no action needed
Wife and children: not relevant to the respiratory assessment
Each visit’s date and reading listed separately: summarise the trend instead
Paragraph plan (thematic order)
P1, purpose: referral for specialist assessment of poorly controlled asthma
P2, the problem now: night symptoms, daily reliever use, falling peak flow, recent exacerbation and steroid course
P3, what has been tried: current inhalers, technique corrected, adherence confirmed
P4, relevant background and impact: ex-smoker, cat, hay fever; time off work and reduced exercise
P5, closing request: assessment and advice on further management
Model opening sentence I am writing to refer Mr Tom Brennan, a 47-year-old warehouse supervisor, for specialist assessment of his asthma, which remains poorly controlled despite good adherence to treatment and corrected inhaler technique.
Model closing sentences I would be grateful if you could assess Mr Brennan and advise on further management of his asthma. Please do not hesitate to contact me if you require any further information.
Key takeaway Notice that the opening already tells the reader why the patient cannot be managed in primary care: treatment has failed despite adherence and good technique. Every kept note in paragraphs 2 to 4 proves that point. If a note does not support the request or help the specialist plan safely, it does not earn a place in the letter.
Common mistakes in OET referral letters
These patterns are common in practice referral letters. Each one is easy to fix once you can name it.
Hiding the purpose Opening with the patient’s history and only stating the reason for referral in paragraph three. The reader should know what you want after the first sentence.
Copying the notes in date order Visit-by-visit paragraphs make the reader rebuild the story. Use chronology only when the timeline itself matters; otherwise group by theme.
Including normal or resolved findings Normal blood pressure, old unrelated surgery and routine vaccinations rarely help a specialist answer your question.
Leaving out what has already been tried Without previous treatment, adherence and technique, the specialist cannot tell whether the referral is justified or what to try next.
A vague or missing closing request Ending with "Thank you" alone. Restate the request: assess, investigate, advise, or take over management.
Note-form shorthand Abbreviations such as "BD", "PRN" or "SOB" belong in the notes, not in the letter. Expand them into full, professional sentences.
Official sources
The test facts on this page were checked against these official OET pages on 27 October 2026.
OET: How to study for the Writing sub-test
OET: Use your reading time to the best effect in the writing test
OET: Is there a word limit for OET Writing sub-test?
OET Writing Guide: organisation and layout
OET: Results and scoring
OET Test overview
Referral letter FAQ
Short answers to the questions candidates ask about structuring OET referral letters.
How many paragraphs should an OET referral letter have?
There is no fixed number. OET says to use as many paragraphs as you need to communicate clearly. Many referral letters work well with an opening purpose paragraph, two or three body paragraphs and a short closing request.
How do I decide which case notes to leave out?
Ask whether the reader needs the note to act on your request or to care for the patient safely. If the answer is no, because it is unrelated, normal, resolved or already known to the reader, leave it out.
Should a referral letter be in chronological order?
Only when the timeline itself is what the reader needs. If the current problem matters most, group information by theme, starting with the problem now, then what has been tried, then relevant background.
Will I lose marks if my letter is over 200 words?
OET says the 180 to 200 word guide is not strictly enforced and assessors do not count words. However, a much longer letter usually contains irrelevant notes, which affects Content and Conciseness and Clarity.
OET Writing next step Find out whether your note selection is working
Write a referral letter under timed conditions and send it for a Writing Assessment. You will see which notes cost you marks, how your paragraph order reads to an assessor, and what to change next.
Get your letter assessed Writing practice tasks
Recommended next steps
01 Sort the notes Keep, summarise or omit before you write a word.
02 Write under time Five minutes reading, forty minutes writing.
03 Get it assessed Feedback on selection, structure and language.
Educational guidance only. Your final result depends on your current level, practice quality and exam-day performance.

## OET Physiotherapy Writing: Referral vs Discharge | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-writing-physiotherapy-referral-vs-discharge.html

How OET physiotherapy referral and discharge letters differ in reader, purpose and emphasis, with one practice patient written up as both letter types.

OET Writing for Physiotherapy
OET Writing for Physiotherapy: referral vs discharge letters
The same patient can lead to two very different letters. A referral asks a colleague to investigate or take over a problem; a discharge letter hands back a patient who has finished treatment. This guide shows physiotherapists how the reader, purpose and emphasis change between the two.
See one patient, two letters
Physiotherapy course
By Dr Ahmed Hesham , medical doctor and founder of OET with Dr Hesham · Published 27 Oct 2026
Before you write
Decide the letter type before you select a single note.
The letter type tells you what the reader must do next, and that decides which measurements, functional details and plans belong in the letter.
01 Who is the reader? Specialist, GP, community team or patient.
02 What must they do? Assess and act, or continue and monitor.
03 What proves it? Lack of progress, or achieved function.
Why the letter type changes everything for physiotherapists
Physiotherapy candidates often ask whether they need a different structure for each letter type. You do not need a template for each one, but you do need to know what each reader is going to do with your letter.
What OET says about the task OET Writing and Speaking are profession specific, so physiotherapists write a physiotherapy task. OET describes the Writing task as a document such as a referral, advice, or a letter of transfer or discharge, written from case notes. You have 5 minutes of reading time and 40 minutes to write, with a guide of 180–200 words for the body of the letter.
Same criteria, different priorities Both letter types are scored on the same six criteria: Purpose, Content, Conciseness & Clarity, Genre & Style, Organisation & Layout, and Language. What changes is which case notes count as relevant content, because relevance always depends on the reader’s next step.
A referral asks for action You are passing a problem you cannot resolve to someone who can: an orthopaedic or sports medicine specialist, a GP, a pain clinic, or another therapist with a different skill set. The letter must justify the request with evidence.
A discharge letter hands over Treatment with you is ending. The reader, often a GP or a community physiotherapist, needs to know where the patient is now, what they should keep doing, and when to act if things change. It is a handover, not a history.
Referral vs discharge: what to emphasise
Use this comparison during your planning minutes. Work through the five rows for the letter type in your task and the structure follows.
Referral letter
Reader: usually a doctor or specialist who has not seen the patient
Purpose: request assessment, investigation or a change of management
Emphasise: the presenting problem, objective findings that show lack of progress or deterioration, treatment already tried and for how long, and the functional impact
Background: include only history that affects the specialist’s decision, such as diabetes before an injection
Close with: a specific request, for example review, imaging or an opinion on further management
Discharge letter
Reader: often a GP or community physiotherapist who will continue care
Purpose: report the outcome of treatment and hand over ongoing management
Emphasise: current functional status and mobility compared with the starting point, walking aids or equipment, goals achieved or outstanding
Home exercise programme: the exercises, how often, and for how long
Close with: follow-up arrangements and clear criteria for re-referral
The measurement rule In both letters, give the starting figure and the current figure rather than every session’s reading. In a referral, the pair shows that progress has stalled. In a discharge letter, the same pair shows what has been achieved.
Practice example: one patient, two letters
This is an invented practice case written by OET with Dr Hesham. It is not an official OET task and does not describe a real patient. The notes are shared; only the outcome after six sessions differs.
Practice example: shared case notes (summary)
Mr Robert Lane, 66, retired bus driver, right-handed; lives alone in a first-floor flat; plays bowls
Goals: return to bowls; reach top kitchen shelves
PMH: type 2 diabetes (metformin 500 mg BD); high cholesterol (atorvastatin); L knee arthroscopy 2015
Referred by GP 01/08/2026: 3-month history of R shoulder pain, no trauma
Initial assessment 05/08: active flexion 100&deg;, abduction 80&deg;, passive range near full; pain 6/10; night pain disturbing sleep; external rotation strength 4-/5; cannot lift kettle with R hand
Treatment 05/08 to 30/09, 6 sessions: education, rotator cuff strengthening, posture advice, activity modification
Version A, 30/09: no progress, so refer
Flexion 105&deg;, abduction 85&deg;; pain still 6/10; night pain unchanged
External rotation strength now 3+/5 (reduced)
Task: write to Mr Sam Hart, Consultant Orthopaedic Surgeon, Shoulder Clinic, requesting assessment
What the referral keeps
Three-month history, no trauma
Range barely changed (100&deg; to 105&deg; flexion) after six sessions
Weakness worsening from 4-/5 to 3+/5, with persistent night pain
Treatment already tried
Diabetes: relevant if the surgeon considers a steroid injection
Omitted: bowls and shelf goals in detail, the 2015 knee arthroscopy, cholesterol medication, living arrangements.
Version B, 30/09: goals met, so discharge
Flexion 165&deg;, abduction 160&deg;; pain 1/10; sleeping through the night
External rotation strength 5-/5; lifting kettle and reaching top shelves; practising bowls
Plan: continue home exercises 3 times a week for 6 weeks; re-refer if pain or weakness returns
Task: write to Dr Priya Shah, GP, informing her of discharge
What the discharge letter keeps
Starting and current range, pain and sleep: the outcome
Functional gains: kettle, top shelves, return to bowls
Home exercise programme with frequency and duration
Re-referral criteria for the GP
Omitted: diabetes and cholesterol (the GP already manages them), the knee arthroscopy, session-by-session treatment detail.
Referral: model opening and closing I am writing to refer Mr Robert Lane, a 66-year-old retired bus driver, for assessment of persistent right shoulder pain and weakness, which have not improved despite six sessions of physiotherapy.
I would be grateful if you could assess Mr Lane and advise on further investigation and management. Please do not hesitate to contact me if you require further information.
Discharge: model opening and closing I am writing to inform you that Mr Robert Lane, whom you referred with right shoulder pain, has been discharged from physiotherapy today after six sessions, having achieved his treatment goals.
Should his pain or weakness return, I would be grateful if you could re-refer him to our service. Please contact me if you require any further information.
Key takeaway The diabetes note shows the whole principle. In the referral it stays, because it may change what the surgeon does next. In the discharge letter it goes, because the GP already manages it and it does not affect the handover. A note is never relevant on its own; it is relevant to a particular reader and a particular next step.
Common mistakes in physiotherapy referral and discharge letters
Most of these come from writing the same letter regardless of the task. Check your plan against them before you start writing.
Writing a discharge summary when the task is a referral Describing all the treatment in detail but never stating what you want the specialist to do. The request belongs in the first paragraph and again at the end.
Listing every session’s measurements The reader needs the starting and current figures, plus any clear change in direction, not a table in sentence form.
Forgetting function Range of movement alone does not tell a GP whether the patient can cope at home. Say what the patient can and cannot do, and what mobility aid they use.
A vague home exercise programme "Continue exercises" gives the reader nothing to monitor. Name the exercises or their aim, the frequency and the duration.
No follow-up or re-referral plan A discharge letter should tell the reader what happens next and when to send the patient back.
Abbreviations from the notes "ROM", "HEP" and "4-/5" are fine in notes but should be expanded in the letter, for example "range of movement" and "home exercise programme".
For a complete discharge task with a full model answer, see the OET writing sample for physiotherapists .
Official sources
The test facts on this page were checked against these official OET pages on 27 October 2026.
OET Test overview: profession-specific Writing and Speaking
OET: How to study for the Writing sub-test
OET: Use your reading time to the best effect in the writing test
OET: Is there a word limit for OET Writing sub-test?
OET: Results and scoring
Physiotherapy letters FAQ
Short answers for physiotherapists preparing for OET Writing.
Is the OET Writing task different for physiotherapists?
Yes. OET Writing is profession specific, so physiotherapists write a task based on a physiotherapy workplace situation. The format, timing and six assessment criteria are the same for every profession.
How do I know if the task is a referral or a discharge letter?
Read the task instructions before the case notes. They name the reader and tell you what the letter should achieve, such as requesting assessment or informing the reader that treatment has ended.
Should I include the home exercise programme in a referral letter?
Only briefly, as part of the treatment already tried. In a discharge letter it is central, so give the exercises or their aim, how often and for how long.
Do I need to include every range of movement measurement?
No. Give the starting and current figures so the reader can see the trend. In a referral they show limited progress, and in a discharge letter they show the outcome.

## OET Reading Part A: Scanning Under Time Pressure | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-reading-part-a-scanning.html

A 15-minute plan for OET Reading Part A: skim four texts, answer matching first, scan for anchor words and copy answers exactly, with a worked practice set.

Reading Part A
OET Reading Part A: scanning under time pressure
Part A gives you 15 minutes, four short texts and 20 questions. This guide turns that into a minute-by-minute plan, shows the exact scan path on an invented practice set, and explains the copying rules that cost candidates easy marks.
By Dr Ahmed Hesham , medical doctor and founder of OET with Dr Hesham · Published 27 Oct 2026
The 15-minute route
Locate first, read second, copy exactly.
Part A tests expeditious reading: finding information fast and recording it accurately. You are not meant to read the four texts from top to bottom.
01 Skim the four texts Titles, headings, table labels and visuals only.
02 Answer matching first Build a map of which text holds what.
03 Scan, then copy Go to one text, find the anchor, copy the exact words.
What OET Reading Part A actually asks you to do
The question most candidates bring to Part A is simple: how do I answer 20 questions on four texts in 15 minutes without panicking? The answer starts with knowing exactly what the task is, because it is not a comprehension test in the usual sense.
The format, from OET
According to OET, Part A has four texts on a single healthcare topic, labelled A to D, taken from the kind of reference material you use when caring for patients: dosage charts, treatment pathways, guidelines and patient information. At least one text may be visual, such as a table, flowchart or diagram. There are 20 questions in three types: matching, short answer and sentence completion.
The clock, from OET
The Reading sub-test lasts 60 minutes, split into two separate periods: 15 minutes for Part A and 45 minutes for Parts B and C. Part A is strictly timed. On paper, the Part A materials are collected after 15 minutes; on computer you submit Part A before Parts B and C begin. You cannot go back to Part A later, so there is no hidden checking time.
Why speed matters
Part A carries 20 of the 42 Reading marks. Fifteen minutes for 20 questions works out at 45 seconds per question on average, including finding the place, reading it carefully and writing the answer. That is only possible if you never read a text in full.
How answers are marked
Each answer is one word or a short phrase, usually one to three words, copied from the texts. OET states that you must use exactly the same form of the word or phrase as the text, that abbreviations are not accepted unless they appear in the texts, and that a response with even one wrong letter scores zero. There are no half marks.
A 15-minute plan you can repeat every time
The timings below are a coaching guide, not an official rule. They follow OET advice to answer the questions in order, starting with matching. Practise with the plan until it feels automatic, then adjust it to your own speed.
Minute 0 to 1: skim, do not read. Look only at each text title, the headings, table column labels, bullet points and flowchart boxes. Give each text a two-word label in your head: for example, A = symptoms , B = treatment steps .
Minutes 1 to 4: matching questions. OET says the first set is always matching, usually five to seven questions, each answered with one letter. Decide from text purpose and audience, not detail. A letter can be the answer to more than one question.
Minutes 4 to 13: short answer and sentence completion. For each question, underline one anchor word (a drug name, a number, an age group, a unit), decide which text it belongs to using your matching map, and scan only that text.
Minutes 13 to 15: protect your marks. Check spelling letter by letter against the text, confirm units and decimal points, and guess any blanks. A blank always scores zero.
The one-minute rule. If one question has taken more than about a minute, write your best guess, mark it, and move on. OET itself advises not to spend too long on one question.
Practice example: following the scan path
Practice example only. The four short texts and questions below were invented for teaching. They are not real OET material and are not clinical guidance. Real Part A texts are longer; the point here is to watch where your eyes should go.
Text A: Recognising hypoglycaemia Hypoglycaemia is a blood glucose level below 4.0 mmol/L. Autonomic symptoms: sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger. Neuroglycopenic symptoms: confusion, drowsiness, slurred speech, unusual behaviour.
Text B: Treatment pathway (adults) Conscious and able to swallow: give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, for example 150 to 200 ml of pure fruit juice. Recheck capillary glucose after 10 to 15 minutes; repeat up to three times. Unable to swallow: follow the emergency pathway and call the medical team.
Text C: Patient leaflet, driving safely Check your glucose before you drive. If you have had a hypo, wait 45 minutes after your glucose has returned to normal before driving.
Text D: Ward reporting policy Record every episode on the glucose monitoring chart. Two or more episodes within 24 hours must be reported to the diabetes specialist nurse.
Practice questions
Matching. Which text tells you: (1) what to do if the patient cannot swallow? (2) what to give a patient who drives? (3) when to contact a specialist colleague?
Short answer. (4) What volume of pure fruit juice should a conscious adult be given? (5) How long should a patient wait after a treated hypo before driving?
Sentence completion. (6) Confusion and slurred speech are classed as ______ symptoms. (7) Two episodes within 24 hours should be reported to the ______.
The scan path, question by question
Skim first. Titles alone give you the map: A = recognition, B = treatment, C = patient leaflet, D = ward policy. That took seconds and you have read almost nothing.
Q1: B. &ldquo;Cannot swallow&rdquo; is a treatment decision, so it belongs to the pathway. Note the paraphrase: the text says &ldquo;unable to swallow&rdquo;. Anchors are often reworded.
Q2: C. The audience is a patient, and only Text C is written to a patient. Purpose and reader decide most matching answers.
Q3: D. A specialist colleague is named only in the reporting policy.
Q4: 150 to 200 ml. Anchor: fruit juice . Your map sends you straight to B; scan for the number next to it. Write the range and the unit exactly as given. Leaving out ml makes the answer incomplete.
Q5: 45 minutes. Anchor: driving , so Text C. Do not repeat words from the question such as &ldquo;before driving&rdquo;.
Q6: neuroglycopenic. Anchor: slurred speech , Text A. This is the spelling trap: copy it letter by letter, because one wrong letter scores zero.
Q7: diabetes specialist nurse. Anchor: 24 hours , Text D. Copy the phrase as written; do not shorten it to DSN, because abbreviations are only accepted when they appear in the text.
Common Part A mistakes that cost easy marks
Most lost marks in Part A are not about understanding. They come from the way the answer is located or written down. Each mistake below is based on the official OET answer rules.
Reading Text A from the top Reading every line of the first text uses several minutes before you answer anything. Skim all four for structure, then scan only where a question sends you.
Repeating words from the question If the question already contains a word, do not write it again. OET gives the example that answering &ldquo;environmental factor&rdquo; to a question about which type of factor scores zero; the answer is &ldquo;environmental&rdquo;.
Changing the word form If the text says &ldquo;unable to swallow&rdquo;, do not write &ldquo;inability to swallow&rdquo;. You must copy the same form that appears in the text.
Dropping units or decimal points When a dose or measurement is asked for, include the unit. Copy decimals as written in the text, for example 2.5 mg, never 2,5 mg.
Adding the text letter Do not write &ldquo;(Text B)&rdquo; next to a short answer. OET warns this can make the answer ambiguous and score zero.
Untidy handwriting on paper On paper, Part A is marked by human assessors. If they cannot read the word, you do not get the mark. Block capitals are allowed, but use them consistently.
How to practise scanning between now and test day
OET recommends starting without the clock: learn the question types and answer rules first, then cut the time gradually down to 15 minutes. The routine below follows that advice.
Week 1: untimed accuracy. Do one official sample Part A with no timer. Mark it strictly: any spelling slip is wrong.
Week 2: anchor drills. Before answering, write the anchor word for each of the 20 questions. Check whether your anchor sent you to the right text.
Week 3: cut the clock. Allow 20 minutes, then 18, then 15. Track how many questions you guessed.
Every session: an error log. Label each lost mark as wrong text, wrong place in the text, word form, spelling or extra words. The label tells you what to drill next.
Key takeaway Part A rewards locating, not reading. Skim the four texts for purpose, answer the matching questions first to build your map, scan one text per question for a single anchor word, and copy the answer exactly as it appears, with the correct spelling and units.

OET Reading Part A FAQ
Short answers to the questions candidates ask most about this part of the test.
How long do I have for OET Reading Part A?
Part A is strictly timed at 15 minutes for 20 questions. It is separate from the 45 minutes for Parts B and C, and you cannot return to Part A once it has been collected or submitted.
Can I use abbreviations in Reading Part A answers?
Only if the abbreviation appears in the texts. OET states that abbreviations are not accepted in the Reading sub-test unless they are in the texts, so copy the words exactly as written.
Does spelling matter in Reading Part A?
Yes. A response with even one incorrect letter scores zero, because you are copying the answer from the text. British and American spelling variants are both accepted.
Should I answer the matching questions first?
Yes. OET advises doing the questions in order. The matching questions are quick and show you what each text is about, which makes the later questions faster to locate.
Reading practice Put the 15-minute plan into timed practice
Use our Listening and Reading practice route to drill Part A scanning under time, then review every lost mark by type.
Practise Listening and Reading Ask on WhatsApp
Recommended next steps
01 Try one timed Part A Use the 15-minute plan from this guide.
02 Log every lost mark Wrong text, word form, spelling or extra words.
03 Drill the weak step Repeat with the clock until it holds.
Educational guidance only. Your result depends on your current level, practice quality and performance on the day.

## OET Reading Part C: Inference and Distractors | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-reading-part-c-inference.html

How to answer OET Reading Part C inference questions: predict before the options, test each choice against the text and see why each distractor fails.

Reading Part C
OET Reading Part C: inference and distractors
Part C questions are built so that several options sound right. This guide gives you an evidence-led elimination method, then walks through an invented practice paragraph to show exactly why each wrong option fails.
By Dr Ahmed Hesham , medical doctor and founder of OET with Dr Hesham · Published 27 Oct 2026
Evidence before instinct
Every answer needs a line in the text behind it.
Part C tests whether you understand what the writer means, including what is implied. The right option is the one the text supports, not the one that sounds most familiar.
01 Predict first Answer the question in your own words before reading A to D.
02 Test every option Look for evidence against each option, not only for it.
03 Keep moving About two minutes per question, then decide.
What OET Reading Part C is really testing
Candidates usually ask the same thing about Part C: why do I narrow it down to two options and then choose the wrong one? The answer is in what the questions are designed to measure.
The format, from OET
OET describes Part C as two texts of around 800 words each, similar to journal or review articles, usually presenting a range of opinions on a healthcare topic. Each text has eight multiple-choice questions with four options, and the questions follow the order of the text. Parts B and C share 45 minutes, and Part C carries 16 of the 42 Reading marks.
The skills, from OET
OET lists the skills as understanding explicit and implicit meaning, identifying main ideas and detail, recognising the attitude or opinion of the writer or people quoted, and understanding vocabulary and reference words such as &ldquo;it&rdquo; or &ldquo;they&rdquo; in context. You also need to follow how ideas relate across sentences and paragraphs.
What inference means here
Inference is what the text commits to without stating it directly. It is still based on the text. If you cannot point to the words that support your choice, you are guessing, not inferring. This matters for clinicians: your own medical knowledge may be correct and still not be what this writer says.
Why distractors work
OET notes that the options often share vocabulary with the text, so it is easy to pick one simply because its words look familiar. Wrong options are usually close to the text: slightly too strong, said by a different person, or true but not an answer to this question.
An evidence-led elimination method in six steps
Steps 2, 3 and 4 follow OET advice: questions come in order and often name the paragraph, you should answer in your mind before looking at the options, and you should look for evidence that an option is wrong as well as evidence that it is right.
1. Classify the stem. Is it asking for a detail, a main idea, someone’s attitude, an implied meaning, or the meaning of a highlighted word or reference? Attitude questions need opinion words; detail questions need facts.
2. Go to the right place and read it fully. Use the paragraph reference as your starting point, then read the sentence before and after. Attitude and main-idea questions often depend on how that paragraph connects to the writer’s wider argument.
3. Predict in your own words. Before reading A to D, say the answer to yourself in a short phrase. This stops a well-written distractor from setting your expectation.
4. Test each option against the text. For every option, ask: where is the evidence, who said it, and is it as strong or as general as the text? Tag each wrong option with a reason.
5. Choose the survivor and mark the line. The answer is the option that still stands after testing. Marking the supporting line makes later review much faster.
6. Respect the clock. OET suggests leaving at least 35 minutes for Part C, roughly two minutes per question. If you are still undecided, pick the best survivor, flag it and move on. Never leave a blank.
Practice example: why each distractor fails
Practice example only. The paragraph, the doctor quoted and the question were invented for teaching. They are not from a real OET paper and do not describe a real person or study.
Practice paragraph Remote monitoring of patients with heart failure, in which weight, blood pressure and symptoms are sent daily from home, has attracted considerable investment. Early trials have been encouraging, although results across studies remain mixed. For cardiologist Dr Leila Okafor, the technology itself is rarely the problem. &ldquo;A reading that sits unopened in an inbox helps nobody,&rdquo; she says. &ldquo;Where teams agree who reviews the data and how quickly they respond, we see fewer emergency admissions. Where they don’t, we simply generate more data.&rdquo; Some nursing groups have warned that monitoring dashboards add to already heavy workloads, a concern Dr Okafor accepts is legitimate, though she believes it can be managed with proper staffing. She is clear, however, that monitoring should sit alongside clinic appointments rather than replace them.
Practice question What is Dr Okafor’s view of remote monitoring? A) It has been shown to reduce hospital admissions for most patients. B) Its value depends on how clinical teams respond to the data it produces. C) It places an unreasonable burden on nursing staff. D) It could allow routine outpatient clinics to be reduced.
Walking through the options
Step 1, classify: an attitude question about one named person. Only Dr Okafor’s words and the reported views attributed to her count.
Step 3, predict: before reading the options, the prediction is &ldquo;useful only if someone acts on the readings&rdquo;.
A fails: overstatement and wrong source. The text says early trials are &ldquo;encouraging&rdquo; but results are &ldquo;mixed&rdquo;, and that is the writer’s summary, not Dr Okafor’s view. &ldquo;Shown&rdquo; and &ldquo;most patients&rdquo; go further than the text.
B survives: a paraphrase of her central point. &ldquo;Where teams agree who reviews the data and how quickly they respond, we see fewer emergency admissions&rdquo; means the benefit depends on the team’s response. It matches the prediction without sharing many words with the text, which is typical of a correct option.
C fails: wrong speaker and wrong strength. The workload warning comes from nursing groups. Dr Okafor calls the concern legitimate but manageable, which is not the same as &ldquo;unreasonable&rdquo;.
D fails: contradiction. She says monitoring should sit alongside clinic appointments rather than replace them. An option that sounds like sensible service planning can still be the opposite of what the text says.
Common Part C mistakes and how to fix them
Review your errors by type rather than by question number. These patterns appear again and again when candidates review a Part C paper honestly.
Matching words, not meaning An option that repeats the text’s vocabulary is not automatically right. Ask what the sentence means, then look for the option that says the same thing in different words.
Ignoring hedging language Words such as may, some, early, mixed and in some cases limit a claim. An option that drops the hedge usually overstates the text.
Confusing who holds the view Part C texts often quote several people. Before answering an attitude question, underline whose opinion the stem asks about.
Choosing true but irrelevant An option can be accurate according to the text and still not answer the question asked. Check it against the stem, not just against the paragraph.
Answering from clinical knowledge Your experience may tell you an option is good practice. The question asks what this text says or implies.
Letting one question eat the clock Spending five minutes on one item costs you easier marks later. Use the two-minute guide, flag it and return if time allows.
Key takeaway In Part C, predict the answer before reading the options, then test all four against the text. Reject options that overstate, belong to a different speaker, contradict the text or do not answer the question. The answer is the option you can support with a specific line.
Official sources
Every test-format fact in this guide was checked against these official OET pages on 27 October 2026. OET can update its guidance, so check them again before your test date.
OET: Reading Part C, the complete guide
OET: Strategies for managing time in Reading
OET: Get ready for the Reading sub-test (format and FAQs)
OET Reading Part C FAQ
Short answers to the questions candidates ask most about this part of the test.
How many questions are in OET Reading Part C?
There are two texts of around 800 words each, and each text has eight multiple-choice questions with four options. The questions follow the order of the text.
How long should I spend on Part C?
Parts B and C share 45 minutes. OET suggests leaving at least 35 minutes for Part C, which is roughly two minutes per question, and splitting the time evenly between the two texts.
Should I read the whole Part C text before the questions?
OET advises starting with the first question and reading to find its answer, rather than reading the whole text first. Read the relevant part carefully, because skimming will not answer Part C questions.
Why do I keep choosing between two options?
Usually because both share words with the text. Predict the answer before reading the options, then check each one for overstatement, the wrong speaker or a contradiction.

## OET Listening Part A: Note-Taking and Spelling | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-listening-part-a-note-taking.html

OET Listening Part A: predict each gap in 30 seconds, write the exact words you hear, handle spelling and abbreviations, with a worked consultation example.

Listening Part A
OET Listening Part A: note-taking and spelling
Part A asks you to turn a live consultation into accurate notes, hearing it once. This guide covers prediction, what to write and what not to write, spelling and abbreviations, and a worked practice extract with the distractors marked.
By Dr Ahmed Hesham , medical doctor and founder of OET with Dr Hesham · Published 27 Oct 2026
Transcript to answer
Predict the gap, wait for the final word, write it exactly.
Part A rewards accurate recording of detail. The right answer is usually one to three words the speaker actually says, sometimes after an earlier detail that the speaker then changes.
01 Predict in 30 seconds Decide what kind of word fits each gap.
02 Listen past the first answer Speakers correct themselves; wait for the final version.
03 Check spelling and form Use the checking time to fix spelling and expand shortcuts.
What OET Listening Part A asks you to do
The real question candidates ask is: I understood the conversation, so why did I lose marks? In Part A, understanding is only half the task. The other half is writing the right words, in the right form, with acceptable spelling.
The format, from OET
OET Listening lasts approximately 40 minutes, with three parts and 42 questions. Part A has two recordings, each a health professional talking to a patient, lasting about four to five minutes. Each has 12 questions, so Part A carries 24 of the 42 marks. You complete a health professional’s notes with a word or short phrase you hear.
The timing, from OET
You have 30 seconds to look at the notes before each recording starts, and you hear each recording once only. On paper you get two minutes at the end of the Listening test to check answers for all three parts; on computer and OET@Home there is a short checking pause built in.
What to write
OET says to complete the notes using the same words you hear, without paraphrasing or changing the information. Answers are generally one to three words. Its own example: if the patient says she was sent to an osteopath, both &ldquo;osteopath&rdquo; and &ldquo;an osteopath&rdquo; are acceptable, but you must not change the word form or add extra words.
What loses marks
According to OET, you lose marks if you repeat words already in the notes, add information that is not in the recording, contradict yourself or make your meaning unclear. Grammar mistakes can also cost marks, and on paper Part A is marked by human assessors, so your writing must be legible.
Spelling and abbreviations: what OET says, and what it does not
Spelling rules in Listening are more flexible than in Reading, but they are not relaxed. Here is what the official guidance says, and where it is silent.
UK and US spellings OET accepts both UK and US spellings in Listening Part A, and says minor spelling variations may be accepted as long as the intended meaning is clear.
But spelling still counts OET also says you may lose marks for spelling mistakes, and that you should be able to spell medical words in common public use, such as diabetes or cholesterol. Treat accurate spelling as the target, not the flexibility.
When you cannot spell a word OET advises writing it phonetically, as it sounded, so you do not miss what comes next, then correcting it during the checking time.
Abbreviations: the official position OET’s published Listening guidance asks you to use the same words you hear, and we could not find an official list of accepted abbreviations for Listening. The Reading rule, that abbreviations are not accepted unless they appear in the text, applies to Reading only.
Our cautious advice If the speaker says the short form, such as ECG, write what you heard. If you abbreviate a longer phrase to keep up, expand it to the full words in the checking time. Do not rely on your own shorthand as a final answer.
Capital letters OET confirms you may write Listening Part A answers in block capitals, as long as you are consistent and do not switch between capitals and lower case.
A step-by-step method from transcript to answer
OET notes that everything on the question sheet is mentioned in order, usually in different words, and that the questions come in order too. This method uses that structure.
1. Use the 30 seconds to predict. Read the headings and the words around each gap. Decide the type of answer: a time period, a body part, a medicine, a number, a job, a symptom.
2. Follow the headings as signposts. When the speaker moves to the next heading, move your eyes with them. If you hear the next heading’s topic, the earlier gap has passed.
3. Wait for the final version. Patients often correct themselves or mention an earlier option first. Write the detail the speaker settles on.
4. Write the speaker’s words, briefly. One to three words, in the form you heard. Do not repeat words already printed in the notes.
5. Check sense and grammar. OET advises checking that each answer makes logical and grammatical sense in the gap.
6. If you miss one, let it go. Keep up with the audio. Missing one answer is better than losing the next three while you think about it.
Practice example: a consultation extract and note gaps
Practice example only. This short extract, the patient and the notes were invented for teaching. A real Part A recording is longer, with 12 gaps and a range of accents. Read the notes first, predict each gap, then read the extract.
Practice notes: practice nurse, patient Mr Daniel Price (1) Night-time breathlessness for approximately ______. (2) Recently started work in a ______. (3) Reliever inhaler now used ______ a day. (4) Stopped preventer inhaler due to ______. (5) Mother has ______. (6) Home monitoring with a ______.
Practice extract Nurse: What’s brought you in today? Patient: My breathing’s been bad at night. I’d say it started about a week ago. Actually, no, it’s closer to three weeks now. Nurse: Has anything changed at work? Patient: I started a new job. I was in a warehouse before, but now I’m working in a bakery, so there’s flour everywhere. Nurse: How often are you using the blue reliever? Patient: Twice a day at first, but this week it’s been four times a day. Nurse: And the brown preventer? Patient: I stopped it. I thought it was making me put on weight, but really it was the sore throat. It kept giving me a sore throat. Nurse: Any family history? Patient: My dad had hay fever, and my mum’s got eczema. Nurse: Do you monitor at home? Patient: Yes, I’ve got a peak flow meter. I use it most mornings.
From prediction to answer
(1) three weeks. Predicted: a time period. Distractor: &ldquo;a week&rdquo;, which the patient immediately corrects. Writing both would contradict yourself.
(2) bakery. Predicted: a workplace, a noun after &ldquo;a&rdquo;. Distractor: warehouse, his previous job. &ldquo;Flour&rdquo; is wrong because it does not fit &ldquo;work in a&rdquo; grammatically.
(3) four times. Predicted: a frequency. Distractor: twice, which was at first. Do not add &ldquo;a day&rdquo;, because it is already printed in the notes.
(4) sore throat. Predicted: a side effect. Distractor: putting on weight, which the patient rejects. Writing &ldquo;weight gain&rdquo; would also be a paraphrase rather than his words.
(5) eczema. Predicted: a condition. Distractor: hay fever, which belongs to his father. If you are unsure of the spelling, write it as it sounds and correct it in the checking time; this is a common word you are expected to spell.
(6) peak flow meter. Predicted: a device. Write the full phrase. A personal abbreviation such as PFM is not what the speaker said, so expand any shortcut before time runs out.
Common Part A mistakes that cost marks
Use these as labels when you mark a practice test. Knowing which type of error you make most often tells you what to drill next.
Writing the first answer you hear Speakers often give an earlier time, dose or option before the final one. Wait until the speaker settles on the detail.
Paraphrasing Swapping in a medical term for the patient’s words, or summarising, changes the answer. Write what was said.
Repeating the printed words If the notes already say &ldquo;a day&rdquo; or &ldquo;pain in&rdquo;, your answer should not repeat them.
Leaving shorthand uncorrected Shortcuts help you keep pace, but the final answer should be clear to an assessor. Expand them in the checking time.
Misspelling everyday medical words Common terms such as diabetes, eczema or cholesterol should be spelled correctly. Keep a personal list from each practice test.
Stopping after a missed gap Losing one answer is normal. Losing the next three because you are still thinking about it is avoidable.
Key takeaway Use the 30 seconds to predict the type of word for each gap, follow the headings, and wait for the speaker’s final version before writing. Write the speaker’s own words in one to three words, then use the checking time to fix spelling and expand any shortcuts.
Official sources
Every test-format fact in this guide was checked against these official OET pages on 27 October 2026. OET can update its guidance, so check them again before your test date.
OET: Listening Part A, the complete guide
OET: Get ready for the Listening sub-test (format and FAQs)
OET: How important is spelling?
OET: Can I write answers in capital letters only?
OET: Reading sub-test FAQs (abbreviation rule for Reading)
OET Listening Part A FAQ
Short answers to the questions candidates ask most about this part of the test.
How many questions are in OET Listening Part A?
Part A has two consultation recordings with 12 questions each, so 24 questions in total. You complete a health professional's notes with a word or short phrase you hear.
Are spelling mistakes penalised in Listening Part A?
They can be. OET accepts UK and US spellings and says minor variations may be accepted if the meaning is clear, but you may still lose marks for spelling mistakes.
Can I use abbreviations in Listening Part A?
OET asks you to write the words you hear and does not publish a list of accepted abbreviations for Listening. Write short forms only if the speaker uses them, and expand your own shorthand before time runs out.
Do I hear the Part A recordings twice?
No. Each recording is played once. You have 30 seconds to read the notes before each extract, so use that time to predict the type of answer for each gap.

## OET Speaking Empathy and Signposting | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-speaking-empathy-signposting.html

Show empathy that sounds genuine and signpost clearly in OET Speaking role-plays, mapped to the clinical communication criteria, with a worked practice example.

Speaking
OET Speaking: Realistic Empathy and Signposting
Empathy in an OET role-play should sound like a clinician noticing a real worry, not a line recited from a list. This guide maps empathy and signposting to OET's clinical communication criteria and shows a weak and a stronger version of the same short exchange.
By Dr Ahmed Hesham , medical doctor and founder of OET with Dr Hesham · Published 27 Oct 2026
The habit in three moves
Hear the cue, name the feeling, then act on it.
Assessors hear only the audio, so your empathy and your structure both have to be audible in your words.
01 Pick up the cue React to the patient's exact words or worried sound.
02 Respond specifically Name the actual worry, then link it to help.
03 Signpost the next step Tell the patient where the conversation is going.
The real question: how do I show empathy without sounding fake?
Most candidates already know they should "show empathy". The problem is that it comes out as the same sentence every time, often at the wrong moment, and the patient's next worry is ignored.
How the sub-test works
OET describes Speaking as about 20 minutes with two profession-specific role-plays of around five minutes each. Before each role-play you get three minutes to read the card, make notes and ask the interlocutor about unfamiliar words. You can refer to the card throughout.
Why your words carry everything
The interlocutor does not assess you. The session is recorded and the audio is assessed by two OET assessors. OET's own Speaking guide points out that, because assessors only hear you, your empathy must be verbal. A sympathetic face earns nothing on a recording.
What candidates usually do instead They say "I understand your concern" after every patient line. OET's Clinical Communication guide comments on a sample nurse who overuses exactly that phrase. Repetition tells the assessor you are reciting, not listening.
What OET's clinical communication criteria actually ask for
Speaking is assessed against Linguistic criteria and Clinical Communication criteria. The clinical communication side has five criteria, each scored from 0 (ineffective use) to 3 (adept use). Empathy and signposting appear in two of them, but they support all five.
Relationship-building
Includes initiating the interaction appropriately, an attentive and respectful attitude, a non-judgmental approach and showing empathy for feelings, predicament or emotional state .
Understanding and incorporating the patient's perspective
Eliciting ideas, concerns and expectations, picking up the patient's cues , and relating explanations to what the patient told you.
Providing structure
Sequencing the interview purposefully, signposting changes in topic and using organising techniques in explanations.
Information-gathering
Active listening, open then closed questions, no compound or leading questions, clarifying vague answers and summarising.
Information-giving
Finding out what the patient already knows, pausing while giving information, inviting reactions, checking understanding and asking what else they need.
What grade B looks like
OET states that candidates securing grade B have predominantly scored 5 out of 6 on each linguistic criterion and 2 out of 3 on the clinical communication criteria.
A step-by-step method you can use in every role-play
Empathy and signposting are easier when you plan where they will be needed. Use the three minutes of preparation for this, not for writing full sentences.
1. Mark the card during preparation
Number the tasks on the card so you can see the topic changes. Then circle the likely emotional moment, for example a fear of needles, a worry about work or frustration with waiting. Those two marks tell you where to signpost and where empathy will be needed.
2. Listen for the cue, not the script
A cue can be a whole sentence ("I live on my own") or a short sound ("Oh..."). OET's guide highlights a sample nurse who missed a patient's worried "Oh" while explaining insulin. When you hear one, stop and respond before you carry on explaining.
3. Name the specific feeling, then link it to help
Genuine empathy has three parts: reflect what they said, acknowledge why it matters, and offer something. "Being on your own after an operation is a real worry. Let's look at what support we can set up." Short, specific, followed by action.
4. Invite the patient to say more
A brief open question after empathy ("What worries you most about that?") turns the feeling into information. It also covers eliciting concerns, so one moment serves two criteria.
5. Signpost every change of topic
Before moving to the next task, tell the patient: "Now I'd like to talk about your medication." OET's guide notes that simple signposts such as "OK", "So" and "Now" work; what does not work is starting each new topic with "um".
6. Organise explanations and pause
Announce the shape: "There are two things to keep an eye on." Give one, pause, check, give the next. Pauses let the patient react, which gives you the next cue to respond to.
Practice example: weak and stronger versions of the same exchange
Practice example (invented for teaching, not a real OET card or a real patient). Setting: hospital ward. You are the nurse. Mrs Patel, 72, had a knee replacement four days ago and is going home tomorrow. Tasks: explain wound care and the exercise plan, and respond to her concerns.
Weak version
Patient: I'm not sure I'll manage. I live on my own, you see.
Nurse: I understand your concern. Don't worry, many patients feel the same. Um, you need to keep the dressing dry and do your exercises three times a day, and also you should take the painkillers before the exercises and call us if the wound is red or hot or there is discharge, OK?
Patient: Oh... right.
Nurse: Um, and the follow-up appointment is in two weeks.
Stronger version
Patient: I'm not sure I'll manage. I live on my own, you see.
Nurse: Going home alone so soon after an operation is a lot to think about. What worries you most about being at home?
Patient: Getting up and down, mainly. And what if the wound goes bad?
Nurse: Those are both important, so let's take them one at a time. First, the wound. There are two things to do: keep the dressing dry, and look at it each day. Does that sound manageable?
Patient: Yes, I can do that.
Nurse: Good. If it looks red, feels hot or starts to leak, please ring the ward. Now, about moving around safely at home...
What goes wrong in the weak version A generic empathy line, followed by "don't worry", which dismisses the feeling. The cue "I live on my own" is never explored, so the explanation is not related to her situation. Several instructions arrive in one breath with no organisation and no pause. Her worried "Oh... right" is missed, and the topic change starts with "um".
What the stronger version adds Empathy that names her actual situation; an open question that elicits her real concerns; an explanation related to those concerns; a signpost ("let's take them one at a time. First, the wound"); an organising technique ("two things"); a check of understanding; and a second signpost ("Now, about moving around"). It is not longer, just better structured.
Empathy phrases that stay genuine
Use them as frames and fill them with the patient's own words.
"It sounds as though [their worry] is what's bothering you most."
"That must have been frightening, especially when [detail they gave]."
"It's completely reasonable to feel [feeling] about [situation]."
"You mentioned [cue]. Can you tell me a bit more about that?"
"Let's see what we can do about that together."
Signposting phrases
Short is fine. The aim is that the patient always knows where the conversation is going.
"First, I'd like to ask about... Then we can talk about..."
"Now, if it's all right, I'd like to move on to..."
"Before we go on, is there anything else about that?"
"There are three things I'd like to explain. The first is..."
"So, to sum up what we've agreed..."
Common mistakes with empathy and signposting
Each of these makes a role-play sound rehearsed, even when the language is accurate.
One empathy line for every situation "I understand your concern" said four times is a script. Vary it by reflecting the patient's own words.
"Don't worry" straight after empathy It cancels the acknowledgement. Reassure with facts or a plan instead.
Empathy too early or too often Opening with "I'm so sorry" before the patient has said anything is not a response to a cue. Wait for the feeling, then respond to it.
Changing topic without warning Jumping from symptoms to medication confuses the patient. Signpost first, then change.
Information dumping after a cue When a patient sounds worried mid-explanation, stop and acknowledge it. OET's guide says it is better not to finish every task than to rush information the patient cannot follow.
Key takeaway Realistic empathy is specific and short, and it leads somewhere: reflect the patient's words, acknowledge the feeling, then signpost the next step. Plan where you will need it during the three minutes of preparation, and let the patient's cues decide when you use it.
Official sources
Facts about the Speaking sub-test on this page were checked against these OET pages on 27 October 2026.
OET: Speaking sub-test overview and FAQs
OET: Speaking assessment criteria and level descriptors (PDF)
OET: Ultimate Guide to OET Speaking Part 2, Clinical Communication (PDF)
OET: What to do on test day (preparation time and role-play cards)
OET Speaking empathy and signposting FAQ
Short answers to the questions candidates ask most about these two skills.
Is saying I understand your concern enough to show empathy in OET Speaking?
Not on its own. Empathy works when it reflects what the patient actually said and leads to help or a question. Repeating one fixed phrase sounds rehearsed, and OET guidance notes overuse of it in a sample role-play.
Which OET criteria cover empathy and signposting?
Empathy sits under Relationship-building, and picking up cues sits under Understanding and incorporating the patient perspective. Signposting changes in topic is part of Providing structure. All are clinical communication criteria scored from 0 to 3.
Can I write notes on the role-play card?
Yes. OET says you can make notes on the role-play card during the three minutes of preparation and refer to it during the role-play. Use that time to mark topic changes and likely emotional moments.
Do I lose marks if I do not finish every task on the card?
OET says there is no penalty for not completing every element, although covering more gives more evidence of your ability. A calm, well-signposted conversation is better than rushing to the end.
OET Speaking next step Practise empathy and signposting on real role-play cards
Use the Speaking practice resources to rehearse the method on a full role-play, then record yourself and listen for missed cues and unannounced topic changes.

01 Mark a card Number the tasks and circle the emotional moment.
02 Record one role-play Five minutes, timed, with a partner.
03 Listen back Count missed cues and topic changes without a signpost.

## OET on Computer vs Paper: How to Prepare | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-computer-vs-paper.html

OET on paper, on computer or at home? See what changes in Writing, Reading and Speaking, how to choose a mode, and a two-week practice plan for each format.

Exam Format
OET on Computer vs Paper: Preparation Differences
OET says its paper and computer tests share the same structure, content, length and marking. What changes is how you read, answer, write and speak on the day, and that should change the last two weeks of your preparation.
By Dr Ahmed Hesham , medical doctor and founder of OET with Dr Hesham · Published 27 Oct 2026
Three delivery modes
Same test, different habits to practise.
Choose the mode your regulator accepts first, then train in the conditions you will actually sit.
01 OET on Paper Printed materials at a venue; Speaking face to face.
02 OET on Computer Listening, Reading and Writing on screen at a venue.
03 OET@Home The whole test remotely, with live proctoring.
The real question: is one mode easier, and should I prepare differently?
Candidates often ask whether the computer test is easier. OET's answer is that paper and computer follow the same test structure, content, length and marking. It adds that candidates who prefer to type may find the computer more comfortable than handwriting. So the mode does not change what is assessed, but it does change the physical skills you need on the day.
Start with your regulator, not your preference OET advises confirming with your recognising organisation which delivery modes it accepts before you book. OET@Home in particular may not be accepted everywhere. Our OET test dates and fees guide lists which major regulators accept OET@Home, plus booking deadlines and fees for each mode.
What actually differs between the three modes
These are the differences OET describes on its own pages. Each one has a preparation consequence.
OET on Paper
Taken at a secure, approved test centre using printed materials.
All four sub-tests on the same day at the same venue.
Listening with noise-cancelling headphones provided; Reading and Writing on paper.
Speaking face to face with an interlocutor in a private room.
You may bring non-mechanical pens, pencils, erasers and a sharpener; highlighters and scrap paper are not allowed.
OET on Computer
Listening, Reading and Writing on a computer at a test venue, on the same day.
Reading completed on screen; Writing typed on a standard keyboard.
Speaking is usually done from home through OET's Speaking Platform with webcam and microphone, on a different day up to five days before or after; in some countries it is at the venue.
An on-screen tutorial runs before the test starts.
OET@Home
The whole test online on your own computer with full remote proctoring.
Listening through a wired headset; Bluetooth headphones are not allowed.
Writing typed on your own device.
Speaking through the OET Speaking Platform with a live interlocutor.
Offered in countries where venue testing is not yet available.
Writing: handwriting vs typing
The task is the same in every mode: five minutes of reading time, then 40 minutes to write a letter of about 180 to 200 words, with the case notes available throughout. On paper, legibility and neat corrections matter, and OET allows all capitals as long as you are consistent. On screen, typing speed and accurate keyboard work matter. Spelling is assessed under Language in either mode, so a typing slip counts just as a handwriting slip does.
Reading and Listening on screen
Reading has 60 minutes: 15 for Part A and 45 for Parts B and C. On computer, OET explains that Listening Parts B and C show one question per page and you click to move on; in Part C you navigate with tabs on the left. OET's tips say that on computer you can cross off answer options by right-clicking and select answers with a left click, while on paper Parts B and C are answered by shading.
Speaking: room vs screen
Both formats have two role-plays, and before each one you get three minutes to read the card and make notes. On paper, you are face to face and can write on the role-play card. Online, the interlocutor shares the card on screen, does an ID and 360-degree room check, and headphones may not be worn. At a computer venue, OET mentions a noteboard for notes.
Booking and results
OET states that computer results arrive in as little as 48 hours after all four sub-tests are completed, with 95% released within six calendar days. Paper results are released from 13 days after the test date, or from five days in India and the Philippines. OET calls all of these timeframes indicative. Computer and OET@Home bookings stay open until seven days before test day.
How to choose your mode, step by step
Work through these in order. The first two can make the decision for you.
1. Check what your regulator accepts
Confirm the accepted modes, the minimum scores and whether results must come from one sitting. If OET@Home is not accepted, it is off the list.
2. Check availability for your profession and country
OET notes that not every date and mode is available in every country. Check your profession, venue and date in the official date finder before planning around one mode.
3. Time a typed letter and a handwritten letter
Write one practice letter each way under 40 minutes. Compare how much time you had left to check, and how many errors you found. That tells you more than a general preference does.
4. Weigh your deadline
If your registration deadline is close, faster indicative results and later booking deadlines can matter. If not, choose the format you perform best in.
Practice example: a two-week adjustment plan for each format
Practice example (an invented candidate, for teaching only). Leila is a nurse whose skills are already close to her target. She has two weeks before her test and wants to spend them getting used to the conditions of her chosen mode. Here is how her plan would differ.
If Leila sits OET on Paper
Week 1
Handwrite three letters under timed conditions: five minutes of reading time, then 40 minutes of writing.
Ask someone to read one letter and mark any word they cannot read at first glance.
Do printed Reading Part A tasks with a pencil only, no highlighter, in 15 minutes.
Practise shading answers neatly for Listening and Reading Parts B and C.
Week 2
One full mock of Listening, Reading and Writing back to back, then Speaking the same day, as on test day.
Two face-to-face role-plays with a partner; write brief notes on the card during the three minutes.
Final check routine: crossing out neatly instead of rewriting whole sentences.
If Leila sits OET on Computer
Week 1
Type three letters under timed conditions in a plain text editor with spell-check switched off, so errors are her own to catch.
Use OET's interactive computer sample tests to learn the layout, one-question-per-page navigation and tabs.
Read Reading Part B and C texts on a screen, not printed, to build on-screen stamina.
Practise right-click to cross off options and left-click to select.
Week 2
One full mock of Listening, Reading and Writing on screen without a break.
Two online role-plays by video call with the card shared on screen, no headphones, in a quiet, clear room.
Test her webcam, microphone and internet connection, and read OET's online Speaking user guide.
Why the plans differ Neither plan teaches new skills. Both remove surprises: handwriting speed and shading on paper; screen reading, navigation and typing accuracy on computer; and for Speaking, either a face-to-face room or a webcam and a shared screen. If Leila chose OET@Home, she would follow the computer plan and also rehearse in the exact room and with the wired headset she will use.
Common mistakes when preparing for a specific mode
These are the problems we see most often when candidates do not adjust their final practice.
Practising only on paper for a computer test Screen reading and typing feel different under time pressure. Use the interactive samples at least twice.
Relying on spell-check in practice Spelling is assessed under Language. Practise with corrections switched off so you learn to check your own letter.
Planning on highlighters or scrap paper OET's test regulations list both as items you cannot bring into the test room. Practise with the materials you will really have.
Leaving the online Speaking set-up to the last day Room checks, ID checks and equipment problems add stress. Read the online Speaking guide and test your device in advance.
Booking a mode your regulator does not accept Check accepted modes before paying, especially for OET@Home.
Key takeaway The content and marking are the same, so choose the mode your regulator accepts and you perform best in. Then spend the last two weeks practising in that mode's conditions: handwriting and shading for paper; typing, on-screen reading and online Speaking for computer and OET@Home.

OET computer vs paper FAQ
Short answers to the questions candidates ask before choosing a mode.
Is OET on computer easier than OET on paper?
OET says both follow the same test structure, content, length and marking. Candidates who prefer typing may find the computer more comfortable, but the level required for each grade is the same.
How is the Speaking sub-test delivered in each mode?
On paper, Speaking is face to face with an interlocutor at the venue. For OET on Computer it is usually done from home through the OET Speaking Platform, or at the venue in some countries. OET@Home Speaking is online with a live interlocutor.
Can I take notes in OET Speaking on computer?
Yes. OET says you have three minutes before each role-play to read the card, make notes and ask about unfamiliar words. At a computer venue a noteboard is provided for this.
Which mode gives results faster?
OET states computer and OET@Home results can arrive in as little as 48 hours after all four sub-tests, while paper results come from 13 days after the test in most regions. These timeframes are indicative.
Exam format next step Practise in the format you will actually sit
If you have chosen OET on Computer or OET@Home, start with computer-based practice so the layout, typing and on-screen reading feel familiar before test day.
Go to computer-based practice Test dates and fees Ask on WhatsApp
Recommended next steps
01 Confirm your mode Check what your regulator accepts.
02 Pick a date Compare booking deadlines and results times.
03 Rehearse the conditions Two weeks of practice in your chosen format.
Educational guidance only. Always confirm delivery modes, dates and rules on the official OET and regulator pages.

## OET Mock Test Online: Full Timed Mock Exams | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-mock-test.html

Full OET mock tests online: all four sub-tests under real timing, Writing and Speaking feedback, auto-marked Listening and Reading, and when to sit each mock.

OET mock exams
OET mock test online: full timed mock exams
A full mock is the closest you can get to exam day before exam day. This page explains what a complete OET mock covers, when to sit one in your study plan, how to read the results against your target grade, and exactly what each mock and practice package includes.
Compare mock packages
Mock packages on the pricing page
The mock cycle
Sit it whole, read it honestly, fix one thing.
A mock only helps if what you learn from it changes the next two or three weeks of study.
01 Sit the full test All four sub-tests under the official timings.
02 Read the report Compare each sub-test with your target grade.
03 Fix, then re-sit Targeted work before the next mock.
What a full OET mock test is
A full mock is all four OET sub-tests, sat under the official timings and marked so you can see where you stand. Skill drills are useful, but they cannot show you how you cope with Listening, Reading and Writing back to back.
Sub-test What OET sets Timing
Listening 42 questions in three parts, using healthcare recordings. You hear each part once only. The same for every profession. About 40 minutes
Reading 42 questions in three parts. Part A materials are collected after 15 minutes. The same for every profession. 60 minutes
Writing One formal letter written from case notes, specific to your profession. 5 minutes reading time, then 40 minutes writing
Speaking Two role-plays specific to your profession. The interlocutor plays your patient or their carer. You have three minutes to prepare each card, and each role-play usually ends at around five minutes. About 20 minutes
Listening, Reading and Writing alone add up to about 2 hours 25 minutes of timed work. On the OET Test on Computer those three are taken on the same day and Speaking is taken on a different day, up to 5 days before or after. On the OET Test on Paper, all four sub-tests are taken on the same day at the same venue. A realistic mock follows the pattern of the test you have booked.
What a mock shows that drills do not Whether your concentration lasts into Reading Part C after a full Listening test. Whether you can let go of Reading Part A when the 15 minutes end. Whether your Writing still selects notes carefully after almost two hours of work. And how nerves change your Speaking when the role-play is the real length and nobody pauses it.
What a full mock includes in our packages Each mock covers Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking. Writing and Speaking are assessed with detailed feedback, while Listening and Reading are auto-marked using answer-key marking. Mock exam allowances are separate from assessment credits, so they are counted on their own.
Full mock exam packages
Three packages for all disciplines, each valid for 6 months from purchase. Every mock covers the four sub-tests; the only difference between the packages is how many complete runs you get.
