How the Writing assessments work Based on Dr Ahmed Hesham's Exclusive OET Rulebook. Detailed Writing Assessment Within 15 Minutes. Criteria-aligned feedback, from the time a completed letter is submitted.
How to pair them with mocks Sit a mock, find the weakest sub-test, then spend the next two or three weeks on that skill with practice exams or assessment attempts before the next mock. The Assessment and Exam Prep packages are listed together on the pricing page.
When to sit a mock in your study plan
OET recommends taking one practice test every 2 to 3 weeks and, in between, working on the skills that caused your errors. It also warns that taking test after test only builds test-taking skills, not your English. That rhythm is the backbone of a good mock plan.
Before the first mock
Learn the format first. Work through an official OET sample test and take the free placement test . A mock sat before you know the format mostly measures confusion.
Baseline and progress mocks
Sit a baseline mock once you know the format, then a progress mock every 2 to 3 weeks. Each gap is for targeted work on the weakest sub-test, not for more full tests.
The final rehearsal
We suggest sitting the last mock one to two weeks before exam day, in the mode you have booked and at the same time of day, so there is still time to act on the result.
Matching the package to your plan One mock suits a single checkpoint or a final rehearsal. Three mocks fit a plan of about six to eight weeks: baseline, midpoint and final. Five mocks fit a longer plan of roughly eight to twelve weeks, or a retake where you need to see a trend. All three packages are valid for 6 months, which covers each of these plans.
Practice example: an eight-week plan with three mocks This is an invented schedule for teaching only. Week 1: mock 1 as a baseline. Weeks 2 to 3: work on the weakest sub-test. Week 4: mock 2. Weeks 5 to 6: the next weakest area, plus timed Reading Part A. Week 7: mock 3 in the booked test mode. Week 8: light review and rest. For the full method, see the OET study plan ; if you are retaking, read what to change after a near miss .
How to read mock results against your target grade
OET reports each sub-test on a scale from 0 to 500 with grades from A to E, and grade B corresponds to a scale score of 350. Regulators set their own minimum for each sub-test, so your target may not be the same in all four.
Listening and Reading: raw marks out of 42 Each correct answer earns one mark. OET says test-takers awarded grade B (350) typically achieve at least 30 marks. Use 30 out of 42 as a guide when you read an auto-marked mock, not as an exact conversion, and look at which part lost the marks.
Writing and Speaking: read the criteria, not just the grade Writing is judged on Purpose, Content, Conciseness and Clarity, Genre and Style, Organisation and Layout, and Language. Speaking has four linguistic criteria and five clinical communication criteria. Feedback that names a criterion tells you what to practise next.
Check the target, then the gap Find your regulator's minimum for each sub-test in the OET score requirements guide , then enter your mock scores in the OET score calculator to see which sub-tests are below the line. Some regulators, such as NMBI in Ireland, accept only one test result and do not accept combined results, which is exactly what a full mock rehearses.
Trust the trend more than one result A single mock can be thrown by a hard text or a bad night's sleep. Two or three results moving in the same direction are a much safer basis for booking or rebooking the exam.
Practice example: reading one mock report This is an invented candidate, for teaching only. Target: grade B in all four sub-tests. Mock 1 shows Listening 33/42; Reading 27/42, with 18/20 in Part A, 5/6 in Part B and 4/16 in Part C; Writing feedback flagging Content and Conciseness and Clarity because unrelated notes were included; Speaking feedback flagging Providing structure and Information giving. The decision: Reading is the only score below the 30-mark guide, and almost every lost mark is in Part C, so the next two weeks go to Part C inference . Writing comes second, with note selection . Speaking comes third, with signposting . Listening is maintained, not rebuilt. Mock 2 then shows whether the plan worked.
Computer or paper: practise in the mode you will sit
OET says the paper and computer tests follow the same structure, content, length and marking, but the conditions are not the same. How you take notes, move between questions and produce your letter changes with the mode, and so does the Speaking set-up.
OET Test on Computer Listening, Reading and Writing are taken on the same day. Speaking is taken on a different day, up to 5 days before or after, at home through a secure platform or, in some countries, at a venue. Rehearse the three on-screen sub-tests in one sitting, and sit the Speaking part of your mock separately.
OET Test on Paper All four sub-tests are taken on the same day at the same venue, and Speaking is face to face with an interlocutor in a private room. Rehearse all four sub-tests in one day, and practise writing your letter by hand in the time allowed.
Inside the learner app you can set a mock to computer, paper or OET@Home mode, as described on our OET practice page . For the detailed differences and a two-week adjustment plan, read OET on computer vs paper .
How mocks differ from free sample tests
Start with what is free. Paid mocks make sense once you know the format and need repeated, marked, full-length runs.
Free resources Full mock packages

Marking You mark your own practice; a new learner account also includes free Writing and Speaking sample results Writing and Speaking assessed with detailed feedback; Listening and Reading auto-marked
Best use Learning the format, and measuring progress if you sit a sample under test conditions Rehearsing the whole exam and tracking progress across several attempts within 6 months
Use the free samples wisely OET suggests taking an official sample to understand the test if you are new, and sitting one under test conditions to measure progress once you know the format. Our OET sample tests guide shows where to find them and how not to waste them.

OET mock test FAQ
Short answers to the questions candidates ask before booking a mock.
What is included in a full OET mock test?
Each full mock covers all four sub-tests: Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking. Writing and Speaking are assessed with detailed feedback, and Listening and Reading are auto-marked using answer-key marking.
How long does a full OET mock take?
It follows the official timings: Listening about 40 minutes, Reading 60 minutes, Writing 45 minutes including 5 minutes of reading time, and Speaking about 20 minutes. On the real computer test, Speaking is taken on a different day from the other three sub-tests.
How many mock tests should I take before the OET exam?
Enough to check progress without replacing study. OET recommends one practice test every 2 to 3 weeks, with work on your errors in between. Three mocks suit a plan of about six to eight weeks; five suit a longer plan or a retake.
Can a mock test predict my OET score?
No mock can promise a result. It shows where you stand under exam conditions. OET says test-takers awarded grade B in Listening or Reading typically achieve at least 30 of the 42 marks, which is a useful guide when you read an auto-marked mock.
How long can I use my mock package?
All three full mock packages are valid for 6 months from purchase. Of the practice packages, Quick Check gives 30 days of access, Exam Prep Pro 90 days and OET Mastery 6 months.
Are the free OET sample tests enough?
They are the best way to learn the format and should be your first step. A mock package adds complete timed runs with Writing and Speaking feedback, which helps when you need to see progress across several attempts.
OET mock exams Sit your first full mock
Choose 1, 3 or 5 full mocks, sit them under the official timings and use the feedback to decide what to study next. Create a free account first to see every package in the learner app.

## OET Speaking Practice Online: 1:1 Sessions | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-speaking-practice-online.html

OET Speaking practice online: private 1:1 sessions with detailed feedback, live virtual-patient role-plays, recorded courses and how to prepare for each one.

OET Speaking practice
OET Speaking practice online: 1:1 sessions and live role-plays
Speaking improves when you perform complete role-plays under time and get feedback against the OET criteria. This page explains how the Speaking sub-test works, what each online practice option includes, and how to prepare so every session is worth your time.
Compare Speaking options
Speaking packages on the pricing page
One practice cycle
Prepare, perform, act on the feedback.
Each role-play is short. What you do before and after it decides how much you learn from it.
01 Prepare for three minutes Read the card and plan your structure.
02 Perform for about five Lead the conversation and respond to cues.
03 Fix one criterion Work on the weakest area before the next card.
How the OET Speaking sub-test works
OET Speaking takes approximately 20 minutes and is specific to your profession. You complete two role-plays in which the interlocutor plays your patient or their carer, and only those two role-plays are scored.
Stage What happens
ID check and warm-up A short conversation before the role-plays. OET says assessors do not rate your ID checks, the warm-up or anything you say during preparation time.
Preparation Three minutes with the role card before each role-play. You can make notes on the card and refer to it during the role-play, but you must return it at the end.
Role-play Two profession-specific role-plays. Each usually comes to a natural end at around five minutes; if it does not, the interlocutor will signal clearly that it is time to conclude.
Marking The sub-test is recorded and the audio is assessed by OET assessors against the Linguistic and Clinical Communication criteria.
Test on Paper Face to face with an interlocutor in a private room at the venue, on the same day as the other sub-tests.
Test on Computer At home through a secure platform or, in some countries, at a venue, on a different day up to 5 days before or after Listening, Reading and Writing.
Why the three minutes matter Preparation is not scored, but it decides how the role-play sounds. Candidates who use the time to plan an opening, the order of the tasks and the point where the patient is likely to need more explanation sound organised. Candidates who use it to write full sentences end up reading them.
What online practice has to copy A useful practice session keeps the real structure: a card you have not seen, three minutes to prepare, about five minutes of conversation with someone who reacts like a patient, and feedback that names the criteria. Anything less is a drill, which is useful too, but different.
What OET assessors listen for
Speaking is marked against two groups of criteria. Practice that only corrects grammar covers a small part of the score.
Group Criteria How it is marked
Linguistic Intelligibility; Fluency; Appropriateness of language; Resources of grammar and expression 4 criteria, each marked out of 6
Clinical Communication Relationship building; Understanding and incorporating the patient's perspective; Providing structure; Information gathering; Information giving 5 categories, each with 3 to 5 sub-indicators, marked out of 3
The OET Speaking tips explain what each criterion looks like in a role-play, and the empathy and signposting guide shows how two of the clinical communication skills change a weak answer into a structured one.
Ways to practise OET Speaking online
There are three kinds of Speaking practice on this site: live one-to-one sessions, live role-plays with a virtual patient on the website, and recorded courses that teach the method. This table shows exactly what each package includes.

Who the sessions are for
Private sessions are listed for doctors, nurses and pharmacy candidates, and are scheduled within your preparation window. Physiotherapists and other professions should check their own course page, such as OET for physiotherapists or OET for allied health , or use the live virtual-patient packages, which are for all disciplines.
When a person makes the difference A tutor hears what a script cannot show: whether your empathy sounds real, whether the patient could follow your explanation, and whether you led the conversation or followed it. Book a session when you know the role-play structure and want an honest view of how you sound, not on your first day of Speaking study.
Live virtual-patient role-plays on the website
The Speaking Starter, Standard and Pro packages are website practice. You speak live with a responsive virtual patient in natural, native-like English, in a two-way conversation that reacts to your questions in real time rather than a one-way recording.

What every card lets you practise Immersive clinical scenarios designed to recreate OET-style role-plays, in which you practise empathy, signposting, reassurance and clear explanations. After each role-play you can read the full transcript, which is often the quickest way to notice long turns, missed cues and repeated phrases.
Website practice and a tutor work together The virtual patient gives you volume: many cards, many openings and many chances to signpost. A private session gives you a tutor's view. Writing and Speaking practice also come together in the Quick Check, Exam Prep Pro and OET Mastery packages , which include live virtual-patient role-plays.
Recorded courses: learn the method first
If you have not yet studied how an OET role-play is built, start with the method. Live practice is far more useful once you know what you are trying to do.

How to prepare before a Speaking session
A session is short, so arrive ready to perform, not ready to learn the basics. These six steps make the feedback land on the right problem.
1. Know what is scored
Read the nine criteria above and the OET Speaking tips , so you can understand feedback that names Providing structure or Information gathering.
2. Rehearse the three-minute plan
On every practice card, mark the tasks, choose your opening line, note one signpost for each change of topic and predict where the patient will push back. Notes, not sentences.
3. Practise your own profession
Work through cards for your profession: nursing , medicine , pharmacy or physiotherapy role-plays, each with model answers.
4. Prepare for emotion
Many cards include a worried, frustrated or reluctant patient. Read handling an angry or anxious patient and the empathy and signposting guide before your session.
5. Set up the room
For any live online practice, use a quiet room, a reliable connection and a microphone you have tested. Poor audio hides the very things you want feedback on: pronunciation, pace and intonation.
6. Bring one goal
Decide what you most want judged, for example "I lose structure when the patient asks something unexpected". Specific goals produce specific feedback.
Practice example: planning a card and using the feedback
This is an invented practice card written by OET with Dr Hesham to demonstrate the method. It is not an official OET card and does not describe a real patient.
Practice example: the card (pharmacy) Setting: a community pharmacy. The patient has been prescribed a new preventer inhaler for asthma. She has heard it contains a steroid and says she will only use it when she feels breathless. Tasks: find out what worries her; explain the difference between her preventer and her reliever; explain how to use the preventer and why to rinse her mouth afterwards; encourage regular use; check understanding.
A three-minute plan in notes Open: name, role, "talk through your new inhaler". Ask: "What have you heard about it?" Reflect the steroid worry in her words. Signpost: "First, how it works; then, how to use it." Chunk: preventer daily, even when well; reliever when breathless. Check. Then technique and rinsing. Check again. Close: agree the plan and when to come back.
Feedback you might receive, and what to practise next
Understanding and incorporating the patient's perspective: you explained steroids before asking what she had heard. Next card: ask first, then explain.
Providing structure: you moved from her worry to inhaler technique without warning. Next card: one signpost for every change of topic.
Information giving: four instructions arrived in one turn. Next card: one point, then a check of understanding.
Fluency: long pauses while you read the card. Next card: plan key words in the three minutes, not full sentences.
Key takeaway Each piece of feedback names a criterion and leads to one change on the next card. Collecting sessions without changing anything between them is the most common way to waste Speaking practice.
Common mistakes in online Speaking practice
These patterns are common in practice role-plays, and each one is easy to fix once you can name it.
Reading from the card Looking down at full sentences breaks eye contact on a video call and slows your fluency. Plan key words only.
One empathy line for everything The same phrase after every patient turn sounds recited. Reflect the patient's own words instead.
Talking more than the patient Long explanations with no questions leave no room for the patient's perspective. Ask, listen, then explain.
Practising without timing Untimed role-plays drift past five minutes. Keep the three minutes of preparation and the five-minute role-play every time.

OET Speaking practice FAQ
Short answers to the questions candidates ask before booking Speaking practice.
How long is the OET Speaking sub-test?
Approximately 20 minutes. After an ID check and a short warm-up, you complete two profession-specific role-plays. You have three minutes to prepare each one, and each role-play usually ends at around five minutes.
What happens in a private OET Speaking session?
It is a live one-to-one session in which you practise different OET cards and receive detailed performance feedback. You can use it as a top-up alongside any course or as a standalone Speaking assessment.
Is the live virtual patient the same as a private session?
No. The Speaking Starter, Standard and Pro packages are website practice with a virtual patient that responds in real time, followed by a transcript and feedback based on OET Speaking criteria. A private session is a live one-to-one session with a tutor.
Who scores the real OET Speaking test?
The interlocutor plays your patient or their carer. The sub-test is recorded, and OET assessors score your two role-plays against the Linguistic and Clinical Communication criteria. The ID check, warm-up and preparation time are not rated.
Which Speaking option should I choose first?
If you have not studied the role-play structure yet, start with the recorded Speaking course. If you know the structure but need more practice, use the live virtual-patient packages. If you want a tutor's view of your performance before the exam, book a private session.
Can physiotherapists and other professions use these packages?
The live virtual-patient Speaking packages are for all disciplines. The private sessions and the Recorded Speaking Crash Course are listed for doctors, nurses and pharmacy candidates, so other professions should check their own course page first.

Choose live role-plays with a virtual patient for volume, a private session for a tutor's view, or both. Create a free account first to see every Speaking package in the learner app.

OET Dentistry
OET Course for Dentists
Dentists sit OET Dentistry. Listening and Reading are the same for every profession, while the Writing letter and the two Speaking role-plays use dental scenarios. This page sets out the English rules of the dental regulators in Australia, Ireland, New Zealand and the UK, and how to prepare with the Modified Allied Health course from Dr Hesham, which covers Dentistry.

Dental route
Check the regulator, then train the dental tasks.
Dentists usually know the clinical content. Marks are lost on choosing the right case notes for the reader and on structuring a patient conversation in plain English.

Who is this OET course for dentists for?
It is for dentists who need OET for registration abroad and want one structured route through all four sub-tests, with personal feedback on the two that are written for dentists.
Dentists registering in Australia
The Dental Board of Australia applies the same accepted English tests and minimum scores as the other National Boards, and OET is one of them. The Australia pathway guide explains where the English test fits in the registration steps.
Dentists heading to Ireland or New Zealand
The Dental Council of Ireland asks for at least B in each OET Dentistry sub-test, and the Dental Council of New Zealand asks for A or B in each, in one sitting. One weak sub-test means another full test, so targeted feedback matters.
Dentists planning the UK
Read the GDC's English language page before you book anything: it names IELTS, not OET. Our OET vs IELTS and OET vs PTE guides compare the tests if you are still deciding.
What is in OET Dentistry?
OET has four sub-tests. OET says Listening and Reading are common to all candidates, while Writing and Speaking are profession specific and reflect workplace scenarios from your own profession.
Sub-test Time What dentists do Dental content?
Listening About 40 minutes, 42 questions Three parts on topics of general healthcare interest; Part A is note completion from consultations, using the words you hear No, the same for every profession
Reading 60 minutes, 42 questions Three parts; Part A is a 15-minute task across four short texts, collected before you start Parts B and C No, the same for every profession
Writing 45 minutes: 5 minutes reading time, then 40 minutes writing One letter from dental case notes, such as a referral, advice, transfer or discharge letter, with a guide of 180–200 words Yes
Speaking About 20 minutes Two role-plays with an interlocutor playing a patient or a patient's relative or carer; three minutes to prepare each card Yes
OET Dentistry can be taken on paper or on computer at a venue. OET@Home also exists, but Ahpra and the Dental Council of Ireland do not accept it, so check your regulator before you book. OET publishes a free Dentistry sample pack, including a Speaking role card; find it through our guide to official OET sample tests .
What OET score do dentists need?
There is no single OET pass mark. Each dental regulator sets its own English rule, and they differ more than most candidates expect.
Destination Regulator English rule for dentists Official source
Australia Dental Board of Australia (Ahpra) Any profession-specific OET, on paper or computer at a test centre. For tests taken on or after 23 April 2026: Listening 350, Reading 360, Writing 350, Speaking 360. Two sittings within 12 months are allowed if no score in either falls below 320, 340, 350 and 350. OET@Home is not accepted. IELTS Academic, PTE Academic, TOEFL iBT and Cambridge English tests are also accepted. Ahpra: accepted English tests
Ireland Dental Council of Ireland OET Dentistry with at least B in each of the four sub-tests, from a certificate no more than 2 years old when you apply. Paper-based and computer-based tests are accepted; OET@Home is not. The alternative test is Academic IELTS with 7.0 in each module. Dental Council: language proficiency
New Zealand Dental Council of New Zealand OET with A or B grades in each of the four sub-tests, passed in one sitting. A pass is valid for two years, and one-skill retakes are not accepted. IELTS Academic, with at least 7 in each band, is the other approved test. Dental Council (NZ): registration
United Kingdom General Dental Council (GDC) The GDC's English language page does not name OET. It names IELTS, including IELTS One Skill Retake and IELTS Online, and its guidance asks for Academic IELTS with 7 overall and at least 6.5 in each area. The guidance also accepts a recent pass in another English-speaking regulator's language test, backed by evidence from that regulator, but it does not name OET, and the GDC says it is reviewing this guidance. Ask the GDC before relying on OET. GDC: English language controls
United States State dental boards We found no US dental licensing route that names OET. Check the requirements of your state dental board and of any programme you apply to. No OET route found

How do dentists pass OET Writing?
You have 5 minutes to read the case notes and 40 minutes to write one letter, with a body of about 180–200 words. OET applies no automatic penalty for writing a little over or under, but a much longer letter usually means notes the reader did not need.
Referral to a specialist Refer a patient to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon, a periodontist, an orthodontist or a paediatric dentist. Say what you found, what you have already done, and exactly what you want the specialist to do.
Letters to a doctor Write to a GP about a finding, or ask for information about a patient's medical history or medicines before treatment. Keep dental terms to what a medical reader uses, and make the question easy to answer.
Letters to non-dental readers OET's own Dentistry sample letter is written to a retirement village, asking for closer supervision of a resident's oral hygiene. Carers and parents need plain, practical instructions, not clinical shorthand.
What the assessors check Six criteria: Purpose, Content, Conciseness & Clarity, Genre & Style, Organisation & Layout, and Language. A clear purpose in the opening sentence and a specific request at the end protect marks across several of them.
Practice example: an urgent referral from a dental practice
This is an invented practice case written by OET with Dr Hesham to demonstrate the method. It is not an official OET task and does not describe a real patient.
Practice example: the task You are the dentist at a general dental practice. Write a letter of referral to the Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery department at the local hospital, requesting urgent assessment of a lesion on Mr K's tongue.
Practice example: case notes (summary)
Mr K, 58, bus driver; married, two adult children
Smoker, 20 cigarettes a day for 35 years; alcohol about 25 units a week
Type 2 diabetes, metformin 500 mg twice daily; no known drug allergies
3 weeks ago: painless ulcer, left lateral border of tongue, about 8 mm; sharp cusp on lower left first molar smoothed
Today: ulcer not healed, now about 10 mm with firm edges; no other mucosal lesions seen
Scale and polish 6 months ago; bridge for upper incisors being planned
Prefers morning appointments; says he is nervous about hospitals
Keep, because the surgeon needs it
Site, size and duration of the ulcer, and that it has grown
Firm edges, and no healing after the sharp cusp was smoothed
Smoking and alcohol history
Diabetes and metformin, relevant to any procedure
His nervousness about hospitals, in one short sentence
Omit, because it does not change the request
Scale and polish, and the planned bridge
His job and family
His preference for morning appointments
Paragraph plan
P1, purpose: urgent assessment of a non-healing tongue ulcer
P2, the lesion: site, size, firm edges, growth, and no healing after the cusp was smoothed
P3, relevant history: smoking, alcohol, diabetes and metformin
P4, closing request: urgent assessment and investigation; mention his nervousness
Model opening sentence I am writing to refer Mr K, a 58-year-old man, for urgent assessment of a non-healing ulcer on the left lateral border of his tongue, which has persisted for three weeks despite removal of a possible source of trauma.
Key takeaway The first sentence tells the surgeon why the referral is urgent. Every kept note supports that urgency or helps the team plan safely; everything else, however true, stays in the notes.
The same keep-or-omit method is explained step by step in OET referral letter structure and the OET Writing tips . To see exactly which notes and sentences are costing you marks, send your letters for OET writing correction .
What dental role-plays should you practise for OET Speaking?
OET Speaking takes about 20 minutes and has two role-plays. You get three minutes to prepare each card, and a role-play usually ends at around five minutes. The interlocutor plays a patient or a patient's relative or carer; OET's free Dentistry sample role-play is set in a local dental clinic.
Dental scenarios worth practising
Explaining a diagnosis and the treatment options, such as a filling, root canal treatment or an extraction
Aftercare advice following an extraction, and when to seek help
Reassuring an anxious patient who has avoided the dentist for years
Oral hygiene and diet advice for a parent whose child has tooth decay
Talking about smoking and gum disease, or with a patient who expects antibiotics for toothache
Responding calmly to a patient who is unhappy about a delay, a cost or a result
How you are assessed
Two assessors score the recording on linguistic criteria (intelligibility, fluency, appropriateness of language, and resources of grammar and expression) and on clinical communication (relationship building, understanding and incorporating the patient's perspective, providing structure, information gathering and information giving). Plain explanations matter more than technical vocabulary: say "gum disease" before "periodontitis", then check the patient has understood.
Build the structure with the OET Speaking tips and empathy and signposting , practise the anxious-patient card with handling an angry or anxious patient , then rehearse dental cards aloud before your private session.
How should dentists prepare for Listening and Reading?
You sit exactly the same Listening and Reading papers as doctors and nurses, so dental knowledge does not help much here. Method does.
Listening (about 40 minutes, 42 questions) In Part A you complete notes from consultations using the words you hear, so spelling and prediction matter. Practise a little every day rather than one long session a week. See the OET Listening tips .
Reading (60 minutes, 42 questions) Part A is collected after 15 minutes, so train fast scanning across four short texts; Parts B and C reward careful reading and eliminating distractors. See the OET Reading tips .
A study approach for dentists
Self-paced, but in a fixed order: confirm the target, diagnose, learn, get corrected, test yourself, then book.
01 Confirm your target Check the accepted tests, grades and test modes on your regulator's own page, using the table above.
02 Take the free placement test Check your Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking level on the free placement test before you choose a course.
03 Learn the method Work through the recorded lessons for all four sub-tests, and keep Listening and Reading practice going throughout.
04 Write from dental case notes One timed letter at a time; send each for correction and fix the same weakness in the next letter.
05 Rehearse dental role-plays aloud Record yourself with a timer, then use your private Speaking session for feedback on structure and plain language.
06 Sit a full mock exam Check all four sub-tests under exam timing with a full mock exam before you pay for the real test.
07 Book OET Dentistry When your practice scores consistently meet your regulator's rule, book OET Dentistry in a format your regulator accepts.
OET for dentists FAQ
Short answers before you enrol. More exam questions are answered on the full OET FAQ page .
Can dentists use OET for UK registration?
The GDC's English language page does not name OET. It names IELTS, including IELTS One Skill Retake and IELTS Online, and its guidance asks for Academic IELTS with 7 overall and at least 6.5 in each area. Check the GDC page before you book any test for UK registration.
What OET score do dentists need for Australia?
The Dental Board of Australia uses Ahpra's accepted test rules. For tests taken on or after 23 April 2026 the OET minimums are Listening 350, Reading 360, Writing 350 and Speaking 360, on paper or computer at a test centre. OET@Home is not accepted.
What OET grade does the Dental Council of Ireland require?
At least grade B in each of Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking in OET Dentistry, with a certificate no more than 2 years old when you apply. The Council accepts paper-based and computer-based OET but not OET@Home.
Does the Dental Council of New Zealand accept OET?
Yes. The Dental Council of New Zealand has approved OET and IELTS Academic. Dentists need A or B grades in each of the four OET sub-tests, passed in one sitting, and a pass is valid for two years.
Which OET course should a dentist choose?
Dentistry is covered by the Modified Allied Health course family, which includes every profession outside Medicine, Nursing, Pharmacy and Physiotherapy. Book OET Dentistry for the exam itself, and practise dental letters and role-plays alongside the course.
What do dentists write in OET Writing?
One letter from dental case notes in 40 minutes, after 5 minutes of reading time, with a body of about 180 to 200 words. It may be a referral to a specialist, a letter to a doctor or advice to carers. OET's own Dentistry sample letter is written to a retirement village about a resident's oral hygiene.

## OET vs PTE for Healthcare Professionals | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-vs-pte.html

OET vs PTE Academic for doctors, nurses and dentists: format, timing, scoring, and which regulators accept each test, checked on official pages.

Test comparison
OET vs PTE: which English test should healthcare professionals take?
OET tests the English you use at work in healthcare, with a letter and role-plays written for your own profession. PTE Academic tests academic English in short, timed computer tasks. Ahpra accepts both, but none of the UK, Irish or New Zealand regulators we checked lists PTE Academic, so your regulator usually decides for you.
Start the free placement test
Compare regulators
By Dr Ahmed Hesham , medical doctor and founder of OET with Dr Hesham · Published 2 Nov 2026
At a glance
Two tests, two very different exam days.
Checked against oet.com, pearsonpte.com and each regulator's own page on 2 November 2026.
01 OET Four sub-tests; Writing and Speaking follow your profession.
02 PTE Academic About 2 hours on a computer at a test centre.
03 Your regulator Its accepted list matters more than either test.
OET or PTE: the short answer
Start with your regulator, not the test. If its accepted tests are only OET and IELTS, as with the NMC, the GMC, NMBI and the New Zealand councils, you cannot plan your registration around a PTE Academic score, however high it is. If it accepts both, as Ahpra does, compare the formats below and choose the test that suits you. Scores and rules change, so confirm them on the regulator's own page before you book.
OET and PTE Academic side by side
Both tests cover listening, reading, writing and speaking, but the tasks, the timing and the way you sit them are very different.
OET PTE Academic
Designed for Healthcare professionals in 12 professions Study, migration and professional registration; not specific to healthcare
Structure and timing Four sub-tests: Listening (about 40 minutes), Reading (60 minutes), Writing (45 minutes, including 5 minutes of reading time) and Speaking (about 20 minutes) Three parts in about 2 hours: Speaking & Writing (76–84 minutes), Reading (23–30 minutes) and Listening (31–39 minutes)
Writing One letter from case notes for your profession, such as a referral or discharge letter, with a guide of 180–200 words A summary of a written text and an essay of 200–300 words
Speaking Two role-plays with an interlocutor playing a patient, relative or carer; three minutes to prepare each card Short answers recorded into a microphone, such as Read Aloud and Describe Image; each answer is recorded once
Listening and Reading 42 questions each, on healthcare topics, the same for every profession Academic item types such as multiple choice, reorder paragraph and write from dictation
How you sit it On paper or computer at a venue, or OET@Home where offered On a computer at a test centre only; it cannot be taken at home
Scores Each sub-test from 0 to 500, with a grade from A to E An overall score from 10 to 90, plus a score for each skill
Results On computer in as little as 48 hours; on paper from 12 days after the test Typically within 2 days
For OET dates and fees, see OET test dates and fees ; to choose between OET formats, read OET on computer vs paper .
Healthcare English or academic English?
OET designs Listening and Reading for all candidates on general health topics, while Writing and Speaking reflect workplace situations in your own profession. Pearson describes PTE Academic as a computer-based academic English test for study, migration or work abroad.
What OET rewards Choosing the right case notes for a named reader, and a structured, patient-centred conversation. Speaking is marked on linguistic criteria and on clinical communication: relationship building, understanding and incorporating the patient's perspective, providing structure, information gathering and information giving.
What PTE Academic rewards Speed and accuracy in short, timed items. The microphone opens on a countdown and each answer is recorded once; for Read Aloud, Pearson scores content, pronunciation and oral fluency. A fluent speaker who freezes on a timer can find this harder than a conversation.
How the scores work
Neither test has a single pass mark. Each regulator sets its own minimums, so the same result can be enough in one country and short in another.
OET: 0 to 500 for each sub-test Scores go up in steps of 10, with grades from A (highest) to E (lowest). Grade B starts at 350 and C+ at 300. The GMC, the GPhC and the Irish medical and dental councils ask for B in each sub-test; the NMC, NMBI, the New Zealand medical and nursing councils and ECFMG accept 300 in Writing.
PTE Academic: 10 to 90 You receive an overall score and a score for each of speaking, writing, reading and listening. Of the regulators in this guide, only Ahpra publishes PTE Academic minimums for registration.
Ahpra minimums for tests taken on or after 23 April 2026
Test Listening Reading Writing Speaking Overall
OET (any profession, at a test centre) 350 360 350 360 Not used
PTE Academic (at a test centre) 58 59 60 76 63
Two sittings of the same test within 12 months are accepted if no score in either falls below Ahpra's floors: 320, 340, 350 and 350 for OET; 53, 54, 60 and 66 for PTE Academic, with 63 overall in each sitting. Tests taken on or before 22 April 2026 use Ahpra's older table. Never convert between OET and PTE scores yourself.
Which regulators accept OET, and which accept PTE Academic?
Checked on each regulator's own page on 2 November 2026. "Not listed" means the page does not name PTE Academic, so you cannot rely on it for registration.
Regulator OET PTE Academic
GMC (UK doctors) OET Medicine: B in each sub-test, in the same and most recent sitting; OET@Home accepted Not listed: the GMC names IELTS and OET as its tests
NMC (UK nurses and midwives) OET Nursing: B in Listening, Reading and Speaking, C+ in Writing; OET@Home accepted Not accepted: IELTS Academic and OET are its only tests
HCPC (UK allied health) Listed professions: total 1400, none below 300 (speech and language therapists 1800, none below 400); test centre only Not accepted: IELTS, TOEFL iBT and OET only
GPhC (UK pharmacists) OET Pharmacy: B in each sub-test, one sitting; not OET@Home Not listed
GDC (UK dentists) Not named; the page names IELTS. Check with the regulator Not named; check with the regulator
Ahpra (Australia, all National Boards except the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Practice Board) From 23 April 2026: Listening 350, Reading 360, Writing 350, Speaking 360; test centre only From 23 April 2026: 63 overall, with Listening 58, Reading 59, Writing 60, Speaking 76; test centre only
NMBI (Ireland nurses and midwives) OET Nursing: B in Listening, Reading and Speaking, C+ in Writing; one result; not OET@Home Not listed
Medical Council of Ireland OET Medicine: B in each sub-test, single sitting; not OET@Home Not listed; check with the regulator
Dental Council of Ireland OET Dentistry: B in each sub-test; not OET@Home Not listed
Medical Council of New Zealand OET Medicine: 350 in Listening, Reading and Speaking, 300 in Writing Not listed
Nursing Council of New Zealand 350 in Reading, Listening and Speaking, 300 in Writing Not accepted
Dental Council of New Zealand A or B in each sub-test, in one sitting Not listed
ECFMG (USA, 2027 Pathways) OET Medicine: 350 in Listening, Reading and Speaking, 300 in Writing, in one test taken on or after 1 January 2025 Not an option: every Pathways applicant must pass OET Medicine
For the main Gulf health authorities we did not find a published English test rule naming OET or PTE Academic, so check with the regulator and your employer; the Gulf pathway guide covers the wider licensing steps. Validity periods and sitting rules are in the OET score requirements guide .
Worked example: checking two score reports against Ahpra
These are invented practice score reports written by OET with Dr Hesham to show the method, not real candidates or results. Both tests were taken after 23 April 2026.
Practice case 1: a physiotherapist with PTE Academic
Overall 70: meets the minimum of 63
Listening 68, Reading 72, Writing 75: all above 58, 59 and 60
Speaking 71: below the minimum of 76
Outcome: not enough from one sitting. A second PTE Academic sitting within 12 months could complete the requirement if it reaches 76 in Speaking and 63 overall, with no score in either sitting below 53, 54, 60 and 66. An OET result could not be added.
Practice case 2: a nurse with OET Nursing
Listening 380 and Writing 360: above 350
Speaking 390: above 360
Reading 350: grade B, but 10 points below Ahpra's 360
Outcome: short for Ahpra, yet the same report meets the NMC rule. A second OET sitting within 12 months with Reading at 360 or above, and no score in either sitting below Ahpra's floors, would meet the Australian rule.
Key takeaway Read your regulator's table for your test date, line by line. A grade B is not always enough, a high overall PTE score cannot rescue one weak skill, and the gap tells you exactly which skill to train before a second sitting.
Who should choose OET, and who should choose PTE Academic?
Your regulator comes first, your strengths second, and convenience last.
UK, Ireland or New Zealand
Choose OET (or IELTS): none of the regulators we checked in these countries lists PTE Academic. UK dentists should read the GDC page first, because it names IELTS.
Australia
Both work. PTE Academic suits you if short computer tasks and a strict timer do not unsettle you and your speaking can reach 76. OET suits you if you communicate best in a clinical conversation and a structured letter.
Doctors heading to the USA
ECFMG's 2027 Pathways require OET Medicine from every applicant. See the USA pathway guide for the other steps.
You already hold a score
A recent PTE Academic result that meets Ahpra's table is a good reason not to switch. If your regulator does not list PTE, do not rely on it for registration.
Comparing OET with IELTS instead? Read OET vs IELTS . Dentists will find the dental rules and OET Dentistry tasks in the OET course for dentists .
Common mistakes when choosing between OET and PTE
Each of these can cost you a test fee and several weeks.
Treating a visa score as a registration score A score that works for a visa or a university may not be on your regulator's list. Pearson says PTE Academic UKVI has the same content and scoring as PTE Academic; neither is on the NMC, GMC or HCPC list.
Mixing providers A good OET Writing score and a good PTE Speaking score do not make a valid set. Ahpra states that results from different test providers cannot be combined.
Using the wrong Ahpra table Tests taken on or before 22 April 2026 are assessed against Ahpra's older minimums; tests from 23 April 2026 against the new ones. Check the date on your report.
Booking the wrong version PTE Academic cannot be taken at home, and OET@Home is refused by Ahpra, the HCPC, the GPhC and the Irish councils. Regulators also name the OET profession they want, such as Medicine for the GMC or Pharmacy for the GPhC.

OET vs PTE FAQ
Short answers for healthcare professionals choosing a test. More exam questions are on the full OET FAQ page .
Does the NMC accept PTE Academic?
No. The NMC says IELTS Academic and OET are the only English tests it can accept, and that it is not looking to accept any other tests at the moment.
What PTE Academic score does Ahpra require?
For tests taken on or after 23 April 2026, Ahpra asks for 63 overall, with at least 58 in Listening, 59 in Reading, 60 in Writing and 76 in Speaking, taken on computer at a test centre.
Is OET easier than PTE?
Neither test is easier for everyone. OET uses a letter from case notes and two role-plays with a person playing your patient; PTE Academic uses an essay and short spoken answers recorded on a computer. Choose the test your regulator accepts that suits your strengths.
Can I combine OET and PTE results?
No. Ahpra states that results from different test providers cannot be combined, and the NMC only combines two sittings of the same type of test.
Can I take PTE Academic or OET at home?
PTE Academic cannot be taken at home. OET@Home exists, but Ahpra, the HCPC, the GPhC, NMBI and the Medical Council of Ireland do not accept it, while the NMC and the GMC do.

Take the free placement test to see where you stand in each skill, then compare the Full OET Courses for your profession, with personal Writing letters and a private Speaking session included.

## OET Study Plan: 4, 8 and 12-Week Schedules | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-study-plan.html

Free OET study plans for 4, 8 and 12 weeks by sub-test: weekly hours, when to take the placement test and full mocks, and how to use free practice resources.

OET study planning
OET Study Plan: 4, 8 and 12-Week Schedules
How long you need depends on how far you are from your target grade and how many hours you can give each week. Pick the plan that matches your starting point, follow it sub-test by sub-test, and let your mock results tell you when to adjust.
Choose your plan
Free placement test
By Dr Ahmed Hesham , medical doctor and founder of OET with Dr Hesham · Published 2 Nov 2026
Three starting points
Match the plan to the gap, not to the calendar.
The same four weeks can be plenty for one candidate and far too short for another.
04 4 weeks: near your target Technique, timing and one weak area.
08 8 weeks: one or two grades short Targeted skill work and regular mocks.
12 12 weeks: building from below B Language first, then exam technique.
Which plan fits your starting point?
OET’s own advice is that candidates whose recent results are already close to grade B may need only a few weeks to get used to the test format, while candidates at C+ or C need more time to improve. If you can study only a few hours a week, plan for longer. Choose from evidence: a recent OET result, a full mock or the free placement test.
Sub-test Time and questions What you do What grade B (350) usually takes
Listening About 40 minutes, 42 questions Part A: consultation notes. Part B: six workplace extracts. Part C: two presentations or interviews. Heard once. Typically at least 30 of 42 marks
Reading 60 minutes, 42 questions Part A: 15 minutes, four short texts. Parts B and C share 45 minutes: six short workplace texts, then two longer texts. Typically at least 30 of 42 marks
Writing 45 minutes 5 minutes’ reading, then 40 minutes to write one profession-specific letter from case notes (180–200 words). 2 of 3 for Purpose and 5 of 7 on each other criterion
Speaking About 20 minutes Two profession-specific role-plays of about 5 minutes, each with 3 minutes to prepare. Mostly 5 of 6 on the linguistic criteria and 2 of 3 on clinical communication
OET notes that the exact Listening and Reading mark for grade B varies between test versions, because grade boundaries are adjusted for difficulty.
4 weeks: near your target
A recent result or full mock puts you at your target in most sub-tests, one is just short, and you know the format. The work is technique, timing and one weakness.
8 weeks: one or two grades short
One or two sub-tests sit a grade or two below your target, for example C+ or C where you need B. There is time for real skill work and a full mock every two to three weeks.
12 weeks: building from below B
Several sub-tests are below B, or your placement result shows language gaps in more than one skill. The first weeks build grammar, vocabulary and stamina. If most skills are B1 or below, the placement test page explains a foundation-first route.
Before week 1: set your baseline
Spend the first two or three days on these five steps, whichever plan you choose.
1. Confirm your target
Check the exact grade your regulator needs in each sub-test, and whether it must come from one sitting, in the OET score requirements guide .
2. Take the placement test
If you have no recent OET result, take the free placement test before week 1. It takes about 60 to 85 minutes and gives an indicative CEFR level for Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking.
3. Learn the format on a sample
OET advises new test-takers to work through an official sample test slowly and carefully. Our free OET sample tests guide and the free practice resources show where to start.
4. Read the method once
Read the Writing , Speaking , Reading and Listening guides before you time yourself, so practice tests a method, not a guess.
5. Fix the end date
OET suggests counting the weeks to your test on a calendar and blocking out work and family commitments before adding study. Check OET test dates and fees so your plan ends on a real date.
The 4-week plan: near your target
Four weeks is for sharpening, not rebuilding. Put most of your time into the sub-test that is short.
Week Writing Speaking Reading Listening Checkpoint
Week 1 Two timed letters (5 + 40 minutes), each compared with a model Four recorded role-plays with 3 minutes’ preparation Part A daily at 15 minutes; one Parts B and C set in 45 minutes One part a day; check wrong answers against the transcript Full mock in the first three days if you have no recent result
Week 2 Three letters; send one for assessment A role-play a day, aimed at the criteria flagged Your weakest part daily: method first, then time Your weakest part daily, plus dictation for spelling Review the mock by error type
Week 3 Two or three strictly timed letters, applying feedback Two role-plays back to back, as on test day One full timed paper One full timed paper Second full mock at the end of the week
Week 4 One or two letters; plan-only drills from case notes Short daily role-plays to stay fluent Light timed sets; no new material Light timed sets; no new material Rest the day before
The 8-week plan: one or two grades short
Four two-week blocks: method, volume, timing, then exam conditions. Spend extra time on the sub-tests your baseline flagged.
Weeks Writing Speaking Reading Listening Checkpoint
Weeks 1–2 Reader, purpose and note selection; two letters a week, one assessed Learn the criteria; three or four recorded role-plays a week Part A scanning drills; Part B method on three texts a day Part A note-taking ; Part B prediction drills Placement test before week 1; first full mock at the end of week 2
Weeks 3–4 Three letters a week; rewrite one using your feedback A role-play a day; work on empathy and signposting Part C inference : one text a day, untimed then timed Part C : one recording every other day, summarising each section Update your error log every weekend
Weeks 5–6 Timed letters of each type; one assessed a week Role-plays with a partner or tutor, both in one sitting Full Parts B and C in 45 minutes, twice a week Full timed paper twice a week Second full mock at the end of week 5
Weeks 7–8 Two or three timed letters a week Short daily practice and one full Speaking mock One full paper a week, light sets otherwise One full paper a week, light sets otherwise Final full mock at the end of week 7; ease off in week 8
The 12-week plan: building from below B
Four three-week phases. Do not skip the language phase: technique cannot carry a sentence you cannot yet build.
Weeks Writing Speaking Reading Listening Checkpoint
Weeks 1–3: language Grammar for letters; turn case notes into full sentences Explain common conditions in plain English; record and replay Daily healthcare reading; summarise Part B texts in one sentence Healthcare podcasts and talks; dictation for spelling Placement test before week 1; first full mock at the end of week 3
Weeks 4–6: method Reader, purpose, selection; one letter a week assessed Role-play structure; three or four role-plays a week Part A scanning and Part B method, untimed first Part A note-taking and Part B prediction Second full mock at the end of week 6
Weeks 7–9: timing Two or three timed letters a week A role-play a day; clinical communication criteria Part C inference; full Parts B and C in 45 minutes weekly Part C recordings; one full timed paper a week Third full mock at the end of week 9; confirm or move your date
Weeks 10–12: exam conditions Timed letters with feedback on remaining errors Full Speaking mocks, both role-plays in one sitting Full timed papers, reviewed by error type Full timed papers; spelling check Final full mock in week 11; ease off in week 12
How many hours a week? Suggestions, not rules
OET suggests finding at least one hour a day to study, as long as the schedule is realistic and still leaves time for commuting, rest, meals and sleep. The figures below are our suggestions; adjust them around your shifts.
Suggested weekly time
4-week plan: around 12–15 hours a week, roughly two hours on most days.
8-week plan: around 8–12 hours a week, with longer sessions at the weekend.
12-week plan: around 7–10 hours a week, with at least half of weeks 1–3 on general language.
How to split the time Give about half your time to the sub-test furthest from your target and share the rest so the others do not slip. Writing and Speaking need feedback from someone who knows the criteria.
Why the mocks are spaced out OET recommends one practice test every two to three weeks, fixing the skills behind your errors in between; test after test builds test-taking skills, not language. A full mock is about two and three-quarter hours of test time, so plan it like a shift.
Common study-plan mistakes
Check your plan against this list at the end of every week.
Mock after mock, no review A mock only diagnoses. Improvement comes after it, when you sort every lost mark by type and practise that skill.
Equal time for unequal gaps Giving all four sub-tests the same hours when one is two grades short.
Writing letters nobody marks Ten unmarked letters can repeat one selection error ten times.
Practising Speaking silently Reading model role-plays is not practice. Say each one aloud, within 3 minutes of preparation and about 5 of speaking, and record it.
Choosing the plan by the calendar Forcing a 12-week gap into four weeks. If your mocks are not moving, move the date, not the standard.
Cramming in the final week New material in the last days adds stress, not marks.
Key takeaway Choose your plan from evidence, weight your time towards the weakest sub-test, get feedback on Writing and Speaking, and space full mocks two to three weeks apart so each one measures real progress.

OET study plan FAQ
Short answers to the planning questions candidates ask most.
How long does it take to prepare for OET?
It depends on your starting level and your weekly study time. OET says candidates already close to grade B may need only a few weeks to get used to the format, while candidates at C+ or C need more time. If you can study only a few hours a week, plan for longer.
How many hours a day should I study for OET?
OET suggests at least one hour a day if that is realistic for you. Our plans suggest roughly 7 to 15 hours a week, but rest and sleep matter too, and a schedule you can keep beats one you abandon.
How many mock tests should I take before OET?
OET recommends one practice test every two to three weeks, spending the time in between on the skills that caused your errors. Repeating tests on their own improves test-taking skills, not language skills, so review each mock before you sit the next.
Can I prepare for OET in 4 weeks?
Yes, if a recent result or full mock shows you are already near your target in most sub-tests and you know the format. Four weeks is mainly for exam technique and one or two weak areas, not for building general English.
When should I take the free placement test?
Take it before week 1 if you have no recent OET result. It gives an indicative CEFR level for each skill, which helps you choose a plan and shows which sub-test to prioritise.
Start your plan Set your baseline, then follow the plan
Take the free placement test to see where each skill stands, then sit a full timed mock in your test-day format. Together they show which plan fits.
Take the free placement test Sit a full OET mock

02 Pick your plan 4, 8 or 12 weeks, from evidence.

## OET Reading Part B: Workplace Texts and Purpose | Dr Hesham

URL: https://oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/oet-reading-part-b-workplace-texts.html

How to answer OET Reading Part B: six workplace texts, timing within Parts B and C, a purpose-first method and an invented practice text with worked answers.

Reading Part B
OET Reading Part B: workplace texts and purpose questions
Part B gives you six short workplace texts, such as a policy extract, a memo or an email, with one question on each. This guide shows you how to find a text’s purpose quickly, test every option against the whole text and avoid the distractors that catch strong readers.
See the practice text
Reading practice
By Dr Ahmed Hesham , medical doctor and founder of OET with Dr Hesham · Published 2 Nov 2026
Context, question, text, options
Know the answer before you read A, B and C.
Part B rewards understanding why a text was written, not spotting the same words in an option.
01 Read the context line The text type tells you how it is organised.
02 Predict from the question Answer in your own words, options covered.
03 Prove the whole option Every part must be in the text.
What OET Reading Part B tests
Candidates often expect Part B to be easy: short texts, only three options. Yet careful readers lose marks here to options that are almost right.
The format, from OET Part B has six short extracts of about 100–140 words, taken from the healthcare workplace: for example a hospital policy, a memo, an email, a notice, a guideline or an extract from a manual. Each extract has one multiple-choice question with three options, A, B or C. The six questions are independent, and Part B carries 6 of the 42 Reading marks.
The skills, from OET OET lists three: the main idea (the overall point of the extract), the purpose (why the text was written) and detail (recognising the important information). A question may be a complete question or an incomplete sentence for you to finish.
Why Part A habits fail here Part A rewards fast scanning for matching words. In Part B, OET warns that a repeated word in an option does not make it correct, and that the right option usually uses synonyms rather than the text’s exact words. Its guide also notes that distractors are partly covered in the text.
No clinical knowledge required OET says you are not required to draw on external knowledge of the topic: the answer is stated in the text, and the text supports the whole option. An option that describes good practice but is not in the extract is still wrong.
Timing within Parts B and C
Reading lasts 60 minutes. Part A has a strict 15 minutes and its materials are collected. Parts B and C then share the remaining 45 minutes, so every minute you spend on Part B comes out of Part C.
OET’s guide: 10 minutes
OET suggests answering the six Part B questions in 10 minutes or less and leaving at least 35 minutes for Part C, roughly two minutes per Part C question.
Our split: about 90 seconds a text
A few seconds on the context line and question, under a minute reading for the point, then the rest proving one option. If you pass two minutes, choose the best survivor, flag it and move on.
Never leave a blank
On paper you shade the circle; on computer you click the option. OET says you will not lose marks for an incorrect answer, and there is no extra time at the end to check, so answer as you go.
A five-step method for purpose and detail questions
Steps 1, 2 and 4 follow OET’s own advice for Part B: read the context sentence, read the question with the options covered, decide your answer, then check it in the text.
Language that signals purpose
Action or new rule: &ldquo;Please ensure…&rdquo;, &ldquo;With effect from…&rdquo;, &ldquo;Staff are reminded that…&rdquo;, &ldquo;This guideline sets out…&rdquo;
Background, not purpose: &ldquo;Following…&rdquo;, &ldquo;As a result of…&rdquo;, &ldquo;In response to…&rdquo;
Language that signals strength
Obligation: must, are required to, mandatory
Advice: should, are advised to, recommended
Limits: may, unless, only if, except, not mandatory
1. Read the context line
It names the text type. Emails and memos usually state their purpose early and the action near the end. Policies and guidelines set out a rule, then conditions and exceptions. Notices say what, when and who.
2. Classify the question
Cover the options. Is it purpose (&ldquo;The email is mainly intended to…&rdquo;), main idea (&ldquo;This extract is about…&rdquo;) or detail (&ldquo;What must staff do if…&rdquo;)? Turn an incomplete sentence into a question.
3. Read for the point
Read the whole extract quickly and say in one sentence who is writing to whom, what is changing and what the reader must do. For purpose questions, look for the sentence that asks the reader to do or know something.
4. Predict, then open the options
Hold your one-sentence answer and look for the option that means the same thing, usually in different words. Never choose an option just because it repeats the text’s vocabulary.
5. Prove every part
Check who, what, when, any condition and the strength of the claim. If one element is missing or changed, the option is wrong. If time allows, find the reason each other option fails.
Practice example: one workplace email, three questions
Practice example only. This email, the wards and the questions were invented by OET with Dr Hesham for teaching. They are not from an OET paper. In the real test each Part B text has one question; here we ask three so you can see a purpose question and two detail questions on the same text.
Practice text (invented): an email to ward nurses about a policy change To: Nursing staff, Wards 4 and 5 From: Clinical Nurse Educator Subject: Insulin and patient transfers
Following two recent incidents in which insulin doses were delayed during patient transfers, the trust’s insulin policy has been revised. From 1 March, a patient on a variable-rate insulin infusion who moves between wards must be accompanied by a registered nurse, and the receiving nurse must check the infusion rate against the current prescription before the transferring nurse leaves. Subcutaneous insulin doses due within one hour of a transfer should be given before the patient leaves the ward, unless the prescriber has documented otherwise. The revised policy is on the intranet. E-learning on the changes is recommended, but it is not mandatory for staff who have completed insulin training in the past year.
Practice questions
1. The main purpose of this email is to A) explain why recent incidents involving insulin occurred. B) inform staff of new requirements for transferring patients on insulin. C) remind staff to complete training on insulin administration.
2. What must happen when a patient on a variable-rate insulin infusion moves ward? A) A prescriber must review the infusion before the transfer. B) The infusion must be stopped until the receiving ward has checked it. C) The receiving nurse must confirm that the rate matches the prescription.
3. Nurses who completed insulin training in the past year A) do not have to complete the new e-learning. B) must read the revised policy before 1 March. C) may transfer patients on infusions without a second check.
Question 1: purpose. Answer B Predict: &ldquo;to tell nurses about new rules for moving patients on insulin.&rdquo;
A fails, background not purpose. &ldquo;Following two recent incidents&rdquo; is the reason for the change. The email never explains why the incidents happened.
B survives. &ldquo;Has been revised&rdquo; plus two &ldquo;must&rdquo; rules are new requirements, in different words.
C fails, minor point and wrong strength. Training appears only in the last sentence, and it is recommended, not required.
Question 2: detail. Answer C Focus: &ldquo;must&rdquo;, &ldquo;variable-rate infusion&rdquo; and &ldquo;moves ward&rdquo;.
A fails, word match in the wrong sentence. &ldquo;Prescriber&rdquo; is in the text, but in the sentence about subcutaneous doses, and only for documenting exceptions.
B fails, clinical common sense. It sounds cautious, but the email never says to stop the infusion.
C survives. &ldquo;Check the infusion rate against the current prescription&rdquo; is paraphrased as &ldquo;confirm that the rate matches&rdquo;.
Question 3: detail. Answer A Focus: the group named in the stem, recently trained nurses.
A survives. &ldquo;Recommended, but not mandatory&rdquo; means they do not have to do it.
B fails, right date, wrong rule. 1 March is when the transfer rules start. No deadline is given for reading the policy.
C fails, contradiction. The rate check applies to every transfer; training changes only the e-learning.
Key takeaway Every wrong option above shares words with the text: incidents, training, prescriber, 1 March. None survives a check of the whole option. Predict the answer first, then accept only the option whose every part you can point to in the extract.
Common Part B traps and how to beat them
When you review a Part B set, label each wrong answer with one of these.
Word matching The option repeats the text’s vocabulary but changes the meaning. Match ideas, not words.
Half right One part of the option is in the text and the other is not. Read the sentence you think holds the answer more than once and check every element.
Background taken for purpose Purpose questions often include an option built from the opening &ldquo;Following…&rdquo; sentence. Ask what the writer wants the reader to do or know now.
Changed strength &ldquo;Recommended&rdquo; becomes &ldquo;must&rdquo;; &ldquo;some patients&rdquo; becomes &ldquo;all patients&rdquo;. If the option is stronger or wider than the text, reject it.
Good practice, not the text An option a senior colleague would agree with is tempting. If the extract does not say it, it is not the answer.
Right rule, wrong scope The rule is real but applied to the wrong staff group, ward, date or situation. Underline who and when in the stem.
A practice routine for Part B
The routine below builds on OET’s preparation advice: summarise short workplace texts, build grammar for dense sentences, and analyse why each wrong option is wrong.
Daily: three texts
Answer three Part B texts at about 90 seconds each. Then write one sentence for each: the main idea or the action it requires. Finally, write the reason each wrong option fails.
Twice a week: Parts B and C
Sit both parts in 45 minutes, aiming to finish Part B within 10. The Part C inference guide covers the longer texts.
Weekly: grammar for dense texts
OET points to relative clauses, conditionals, participle clauses and long noun phrases. Rewrite one complex policy sentence as two plain ones.
Always: an error log
Count your mistakes by trap type, not by question. Combine Part B work with Part A scanning and the wider Reading tips .

OET: 5 easy steps to speed up during Reading Part B

OET: Seven tips to improve your Reading score

OET Reading Part B FAQ
Short answers to the questions candidates ask most about this part of the test.
How many questions are in OET Reading Part B?
Part B has six short workplace texts of about 100 to 140 words each, with one three-option multiple-choice question per text. It is worth 6 of the 42 Reading marks.
How long should I spend on Reading Part B?
Parts B and C share 45 minutes. OET suggests answering the six Part B questions in 10 minutes or less so that you leave at least 35 minutes for Part C.
What kinds of texts appear in Reading Part B?
Short texts from the healthcare workplace, such as a hospital policy, a memo, an email, a notice, a guideline or an extract from a manual. A context sentence tells you the text type before you read.
Should I use my clinical knowledge in Part B?
No. OET says you are not required to draw on external knowledge of the topic. The answer is stated in the text, so an option that is clinically sensible but not in the extract is wrong.
Do I lose marks for a wrong answer in OET Reading?
No. OET says you will not lose marks for an incorrect answer, so choose the best remaining option rather than leaving a question blank.
Reading practice Practise Part B against the 10-minute target
Work on Part B texts one at a time, then sit Parts B and C together under the 45-minute limit and log every lost mark by trap type.
Practise Listening and Reading Reading Part C guide
Recommended next steps
01 Three texts a day About 90 seconds each, then summarise.
02 Prove every option Who, what, when, condition and strength.
03 Time B and C together 10 minutes for B, 35 or more for C.
Educational guidance only. Your result depends on your current level, practice quality and performance on the day.
About the author Dr Ahmed Hesham is a medical doctor and OET educator who has coached doctors, nurses and allied health professionals preparing for OET since 2018. More about Dr Hesham .
